O R D E R 
 
 
 
  DIPANKAR DATTA, J. 
 
 
 
1. Rajasthan Housing Board , by presenting this special leave petition , 
challenges a judgment and order dated 06th July, 20261 passed by the 
High Court of Judicature for Rajasthan, Bench at Jaipur 2. The 
impugned judgment dismissed an application 3 under Article 227 of 
the Constitution preferred by the Rajasthan Housing Board along with 
the State of Rajasthan  and the Special Officer, Urban Development 
and Housing Department, Rajasthan.  
2. In the writ petition, two orders were assailed: first, an order dated 
 
1 impugned judgment 
2 High Court 
3 S.B. Civil Writ Petition No. 4122/2026 

--- Page 21 ---
2 
 
26th May, 2025 of the Land Acquisition Rehabilitation and 
Resettlement Authority 4, headquartered at Jaipur , allowing the 
reference sought by the first respondent under Section 64 of the Right 
to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, 
Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013 5; and, secondly, an order 
dated 12 th September, 2025 passed by the LARRA making a minor 
modification in favour of the first respondent while allowing its review 
petition.  
3. The assail to the said two orders was spurned by the High Court by 
holding that the writ petition was not maintainable in view of the 
appellate remedy made available by sub-section (1) of Section 74 of 
the 2013 Act. The High Court further held that even if the writ petition 
were to be treated as an appeal under Section 74, the proviso thereof 
would be attracted on account of the belated approach . In terms of 
such proviso,  no appeal  which is  presented 60 days beyond the 
prescribed period of limitation of 60 days could be entertained.  
Ultimately, resting on such premise, it was held that the right of the 
petitioners before the High Court even to maintain an appeal would 
stand foreclosed after expiry of the maximum permissible period for 
condonation of delay  and, therefore, the writ petition could not be 
treated as an appeal. 
4. Appearing in support of the special leave petition, Mr. Anuj Bhandari, 
learned counsel sought to rely on the decision of a coordinate Bench 
of this Court in Deputy Commissioner and Special Land 
 
4 LARRA 
5 2013 Act 

--- Page 22 ---
3 
 
Acquisition Officer v. S.V. Global Mill Limited6. He contends that 
the period of 60 days stipulated in the proviso to Section 74 of the 
2013 Act has been held not to be mandatory. It does not  foreclose 
the high c ourts from condon ing delay beyond that period upon 
sufficient cause being shown. He, thus, urges that the decision in S.V. 
Global Mill Limited (supra) (which went unnoticed by the High 
Court) having brought about a radical shift in judicial thinking , the 
Rajasthan Housing Board may be granted the liberty of now 
approaching the appellate forum with an application for condonation 
of delay. 
5. We have perused the decision in S.V. Global Mill Limited  (supra). 
Instead of quoting the relevant passages from such decision, we  
consider it proper to summarize what has been reasoned there 
(particularly in paragraphs 13, 35, 36, 59, 76, 78 and 79 ). The 
coordinate Bench was of the opinion that the 2013 Act is a beneficial 
legislation and the Courts must make a conscious endeavour to give 
effect to its avowed objectives ; Section 74 of the 2013 Act provides 
for a period of 60 days from the date of the award for filing an appeal 
before the high courts; the starting point for computation of the said 
60 days being the date of receipt of the said award by the aggrieved 
person, the proviso to Section 74 allows an appeal to be filed within 
a further period of 60 days ; while such proviso does not extend the 
period of limitation prescribed for filing the appeal, it brings a delayed 
filing within the ambit of Section 74(1) ; being a mere proviso, such 
 
6 2026 SCC OnLine SC 171 

--- Page 23 ---
4 
 
proviso cannot be interpreted to mean otherwise ; Section 74, as a 
whole, does not involve the exercise of power conferred to the Court 
under Section 5 of the Limitation Act, 19637; there is not much 
difference between the main provision contained in Section 74(1) and 
its proviso; Section 74 provides only one period of limitation, meaning 
thereby that the other one mentioned under the proviso gets 
subsumed within the period provided under Section 74(1) ; Section 
103 of the 2013 Act facilitates borrowing from other enactments, and 
clarifies that the provisions of the 2013 Act are in addition to other 
laws, and not in derogation thereof; the language of Section 29(2) of 
the Limitation Act indicates the intention of the Legislature to extend 
the application of Sections 4 to 24 thereof to all special or local laws 
and a specific exclusion alone would take away its application ; the 
2013 Act, being a special law, there is nothing in Section 74 
suggesting an exclusion of Sections 4 to 24 ; and, hence, application 
of the Limitation Act is not excluded qua the 2013 Act. 
6. We had expressed reservation as to whether S.V. Global Mill 
Limited (supra) lays down correct law , having the efficacy of a 
binding precedent. The immediate response of Mr. Bhandari was that 
in such case, a reference to a larger Bench would be the proper course 
for us to follow.  
7. A reference is not warranted in the present facts and circumstances . 
The ratio of S.V. Global Mill Limited (supra) does not apply here, 
for reasons we propose to record hereafter. However, at the same 
 
7 Limitation Act 

--- Page 24 ---
5 
 
time, we wish also to briefly observe why  in our opinion  such 
precedent does not commend our acceptance. 
8. A whole lot of enactments, viz. the Securities and Exchange Board of 
India Act, 1992 (Section 15 -Z), the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 
19968 (Section 34), the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999 9 
(Section 35), the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002 (Section 
42), the Electricity Act, 2003 10 (Section 125), the Companies Act, 
201311 (Sections 421 and 423), and the Insolvency and Bankruptcy 
Code, 201612 (Sections 61 and 62) prescribe the period of limitation 
for filing appeals/applications. The relevant provisions contain in-built 
provisions as well , prescribing the outer limit beyond which 
condonation of delay is not permissible.  The words used  in such 
provisions like “but not thereafter” or “not exceeding” as suffix/prefix 
to a particular period of time have been uniformly held by separate 
Benches of this Court (majorly in combination of 2 -Judges, and 3-
Judges in the rest ) to constitute a legislative command exceeding 
which the courts have no power to condone delay in presentation of 
an appeal/application. 
9. We may notice how such enactments, along with others, have been 
considered by this Court . Law seems to have been consistently laid 
down that each enactment is a code in itself and beyond the maximum 
condonable period  permitted thereby , no time barred 
appeal/application can be entertained by taking the aid of Section 5

of the Limitation Act . Reference may, inter alia , be made to the

Limited v. Raj Kumar Banerjee  & Ors.26 dealing with Section 61

10. Needless to observe, the language of sub-section (1) of Section 74 of 
the 2013 Act is in pari materia with the provisions of the statutes 
considered by this Court in the precedents cited above . It would, 
therefore, appear that the decision of the coordinate Bench in S.V. 
Global Mill Limited (supra) does not accord with the precedents 
dealing with similar provisions as to limitation.  
11. Moreover, the decision in S.V. Global Mill Limited (supra) effectively 
renders the proviso to sub-section (1) of Section 74 otiose. 
Consequent upon S ection 5 of the Limitation Act  being made 
applicable to appeals carried from awards under the main part of sub-
section (1) of Section 74 of the 2013 Act,  any appellant is now 
permitted to show “sufficient cause” for not preferring such an appeal 
within the prescribed time before the high courts . As a sequel, the 
outer limit of 120 days that the section prescribes is denuded of all 
its meaning. The net effect is that a parliamentary prescription stands 
altered by a judicial interpretation, giving impetus to belated appeals 
under Section 74 of the 2013 Act being filed and to the plea that any 
 
26 (2025) 9 SCC 483 (2-J) 
27 (2025) SCC OnLine SC 2484 (2-J) 
28 (2026) SCC OnLine SC 1097 (2-J) 

--- Page 27 ---
8 
 
delay, howsoever inordinate, be condoned. On a bare textual reading 
of sub-section (1) of Section 74 of the 2013  Act, it is manifest that 
the legislature did not intend condonation of delay beyond the period 
of 120 days and thus, impliedly, if not expressly , excluded 
applicability of Section 5 of the Limitation Act . Had a contrary 
intention been contemplated, the legislature would have employed 
appropriate language to convey the same.  
12. Since a different view was taken by this Court in S.V. Global Mill 
Limited (supra) relying on sub-section (2) of Section 29 of the 
Limitation Act, let us now consider whether such view can also be 
sustained. 
13. Sub-section (2) of Section 29 of the Limitation Act reads as follows: 
Section 29. Savings  
(1) *** 
(2) Where any special or local law prescribes for any suit, appeal or 
application a period of limitation different from the period prescribed 
by the Schedule, the provisions of Section 3 shall apply as if such 
period were the period prescribed by the Schedule and for the purpose 
of determining any period of limitation prescribed for any suit, appeal 
or application by any special or local law, the provisions contained in 
Sections 4 to 24 (inclusive) shall apply only insofar as, and to the 
extent to which, they are not expressly excluded by such special or 
local law. 
 
14. Hukumdev Narain Yadav v. Lal Narain Mishra29 is considered an 
authority on the question of the true interpretation of sub-section (2) 
of Section 29 of the Limitation Act. It was held there that even in a 
case where the special law does not exclude the provisions of Sections 
4 to 24 of the Limitation Act by an express reference, it would 
nonetheless be open to the court to examine whether and to what 
 
29 (1974) 2 SCC 133 (3-J) 

--- Page 28 ---
9 
 
extent the nature of those provisions or the nature of the subject -
matter and scheme of the special law exclude their operation. 
15. The principle of law laid down in the said decision has since been 
followed/relied upon in several subsequent decisions of this Court 
including Anwari Basavaraj Patil  & Ors.  v. Siddaramaiah  & 
Ors.30 and Gopal Sardar v. Karuna Sardar31. The coordinate Bench 
in S.V. Global Mill Limited (supra) was not referred to either of 
these two decisions.  
16. Even otherwise, Hukumdev Narain Yadav  (supra) is a judgment 
delivered by a 3-Judge Bench. The ratio laid down therein is binding 
on any Bench of lesser strength. However, such ratio was 
distinguished in S.V. Global Mill Limited (supra) on the specious 
ground that the dispute in Hukumdev Narain Yadav  (supra) 
pertained to an election dispute. In our view, the nature of the dispute 
and/or the subject matter of the statute from which the lis originates 
is irrelevant while interpreting sub-section (2) of Section 29 of the 
Limitation Act. What is relevant is the  scheme of the statute under 
consideration, in light of the  principle of law settled by the larger 
Bench. The test would be , whether in the absence of express 
exclusion, application of the provisions of Sections 4 to 24 of the 
Limitation Act can be excluded by necessary implication or not? To 
construe sub-section (2) of Section 29 of the Limitation Act only if 
there is an express exclusion would run contrary to the view taken by 
the larger Bench. Also, one other aspect seems to have escaped the 
 
30 (1993) 1 SCC 636 (2-J) 
31 (2004) 4 SCC 252 (2-J) 

--- Page 29 ---
10 
 
attention of the coordinate Bench. Applying Section 5 of the Limitation 
Act to a time-barred appeal under sub-section (1) of Section 74 of the 
2013 Act, on the premise that the 2013 Act is a beneficial legislation, 
would occasion reverse prejudice. The State/acquiring bodies would 
also become entitled to seek condonation of inordinate delay, much 
to the prejudice and detriment of the landowners . In our considered 
opinion, such an  interpretative exercise  ought best to  have been 
avoided.    
17. Be that as it may, our understanding of sub-section (2) of Section 29 
of the Limitation Act as interpreted by judicial precedents is this. Sub-
section (2) of Section 29 provides that Sections 4 to 24 of the 
Limitation Act shall apply to proceedings under any special or local 
law prescribing a period of limitation different from the Schedule to 
the Limitation Act , save where their application – and in particular 
Section 5 – is excluded expressly or by necessary implication. The 
proviso to sub -section (1) of  Section 74 of the 2013 Act is in the 
nature of a special in-built provision akin to Section 5 of the Limitation 
Act, permitting condonation of delay subject, however, to a statutory 
cap. Sub-section (1) of Section 74, though part of the 2013 Act which 
is a special law, admits of no ambiguity and is incapable of two 
constructions. Application of Sections 4 to 24 is not available in view 
of such an unambiguous provision and, therefore, no further 
condonation outside the second phase of time-limit of 60 days is 
permissible in case of a time -barred appeal under Section 74 of the 
2013 Act. The question of application of Section 5 of the Limitation 
Act to such an appeal, thus, does not arise.      

--- Page 30 ---
11 
 
18. In this connection, it would also be profitable to note the decision in  
CST v. Parson Tools and Plants32 where this Court had the occasion 
to hold:  
16. If the legislature wilfully omits to incorporate something of an 
analogous law in a subsequent statute, or even if there is a casus 
omissus in a statute, the language of which is otherwise plain and 
unambiguous, the Court is not competent to supply the omission by 
engrafting on it or introducing in it, under the guise of interpretation, 
by analogy or implication, something what it thinks to be a general 
principle of justice and equity. To do so “would be entrenching upon 
the preserves of legislature”33, the primary function of a Court of law 
being jus dicere and not jus dare. 
 
19. The principle in Parson Tools and Plants (supra) is equally available 
in its converse  – where the competent legislature has consciously 
engrafted in the subsequent statute what was absent or was an 
omission in an earlier one, it is not open to the court to undo the 
legislative choice by an interpretive exercise.  
20. Reading Section 74 of the 2013 in juxtaposition with Section 54 of the 
erstwhile Land Acquisition Act, 1894 and also having regard to the 
scheme of the 2013 Act, we have no hesitation in holding that the 
period of 120 days in Section 74 is inflexible and rigid and cannot be 
read in a manner so as to permit an y aggrieved person to approach 
the relevant high court with an appeal which is barred even by a single 
day’s delay. Even this Court in exercise of its power under Article 142 
cannot condone the delay although, in a fit and proper case, a party 
may seek exemption from application of the laws of limitation.  
21. Reverting to Mr. Bhandari’s plea for re ferring the decision in S.V. 
Global Mill Limited (supra) for reconsideration by a larger Bench, it 
 
32 (1975) 4 SCC 22 (3-J) 
33 Prem Nath L. Ganesh v. Prem Nath L. Ram Nath : AIR 1963 Punjab 62 (Tek Chand, J.) 

--- Page 31 ---
12 
 
is, indeed, not an available option. Given the uniform interpretation 
of pari materia provisions as to limitation placed by several Benches 
of this Court in a long line of decisions and in keeping with the doctrine 
of stare decisis, the two -Judge Bench in S.V. Global Mill Limited 
(supra) ought not to have placed a discordant construction on sub -
section (1) of Section 74 of the 2013 Act ; instead, since such 
consistent views of this Court as well as the long standing and well 
accepted ratio of Hukumdev Narain Yadav  (supra) were being 
departed from,  it could have itself referred the matter for 
consideration by a larger Bench . Being bound by  the doctrine of 
precedents, laid down by larger Benches, we decline a reference. 
22. Having observed thus, we now revert to the case at hand. 
23. Assuming that the decision in S.V. Global Mill Limited (supra) lays 
down the law correctly, the ratio thereof is inapplicable here because 
the Rajasthan Housing Board did not avail the appellate remedy 
provided by Section 74 of the 2013 Act with a time-barred appeal; on 
the contrary, it had invoked the jurisdiction of the High Court under 
Article 227 of the Constitution . Having failed /neglected/omitted to 
avail the appellate remedy either within the maximum condonable 
period or even thereafter, seeking condonation of delay  by applying 
under Section 5 of the Limitation Act , the High Court in our opinion 
was perfectly justified in spurning the challenge. There is, thus, no 
ground to cause interference with such reasoned decision of the High 
Court. 
24. In light of the above discussion, there is no reason to  refer the 
decision in S.V. Global Mill Limited (supra) to a larger Bench. We, 

--- Page 32 ---
13 
 
however, hasten to add that pending time -barred appeals under 
Section 74 of the 2013 Act may be decided by the relevant high courts 
in accordance with law. 
25. The special leave petition, accordingly, stands dismissed. 
26. Connected applications, if any, stand disposed of.

3. The learned counsel for the applicant-husband submits that the
first party has paid an amount of Rs.20,00,000/- and has handed
over  the  jewellery  of  the  respondent  No.2,  to  her  with  due
acknowledgement  taken  and  has  also  remitted  Rs.50,000/-  as
amounts due to the educational expenses of their only son incurred
till date. The appellant also agrees to pay the amount of Rs.7,000/-
to the respondent for the maintenance of the child till he attains the
age of 18. Insofar as the maintenance agreed to be paid at the rate
of Rs.10,000/- to the respondent, it is submitted that the respondent
has  remarried  and  hence  she  is  not  entitled  to  maintenance;
admitted by her too.
4. At  the  last  date  of  hearing  learned  counsel  for  the  2nd
respondent submitted that there are many  more things that the
applicant has to comply with and hence we directed the parties to
be present in person. T oday, when the matter was taken up, the
grievance was with respect to the entire jewellery not having been
handed  over.  The  learned  counsel  for  the  applicant,  however,
pointed out the acknowledgment, duly signed by the 2 nd respondent
with respect to the jewellery handed over to her. We find that there
is  no  reservation  expressed  in  the  acknowledgement  by  the  2nd
respondent regarding the claim of further jewellery withheld by the
applicant-husband.

--- Page 40 ---
8
5. Insofar  as  the  child’s  maintenance,  the  applicant-husband
undertakes  to  remit  the  amounts  scrupulously.  The  applicant-
husband also has taken out a Medi-claim policy to cover medical
expense of his son, which he shall renew every year till the son
obtains a job. The other undertaking made with respect to the child,
is in future after the child attains majority. Insofar as the claim of
jewellery, we accept the contention of the applicant that the entire
jewellery  has  been  handed  over;  especially  going  by  the
acknowledgement, which does not express any reservation.
6. In the above circumstances, we are of the definite opinion that
the marriage has broken down irretrievably. We invoke our powers
under Article 142 of the Constitution of India to grant divorce to the
parties on the ground of irretrievable breakdown of marriage.
7. The parties having agreed to settle the matter on the specific
terms herein above noticed, we are of the opinion that the cases
pending against each other, be it civil or criminal, shall stand closed;
especially those referred to in clause (P) of the settlement extracted
hereinabove.
8. The husband’s contention is also with respect to a release deed
having not been executed as pointed out from clause (C) of the
settlement.  The  learned  counsel  for  the  respondent,  however,
submits that there is nothing stated in the said clause, as to the

--- Page 41 ---
9
relinquishment  being  made  in  favour  of  the  applicant.  We  only
notice the contention to reject it. When the settlement was arrived
at between two parties and one agrees to relinquish her right over a
property in which they have common ownership, the relinquishment
should be in favour of the other party. We, hence, direct the 2 nd
respondent to immediately execute the relinquishment deed within
a period of two months, the expenses of which shall be borne by the
applicant herein.
9. We make it clear that on any breach of the terms of settlement,
either  parties  will  be  permitted  to  approach  this  Court  with  an
appropriate application for initiating contempt proceedings.
10. The matter stands disposed of.
11. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand rejected.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. Heard  Mr.  D.D.  Tripathi,  learned  counsel  for  the
petitioner-complainant(sister of the deceased), Mr. Yashveer
Singh, learned counsel for the State and Mr. Ajay Vikram
Singh, learned counsel for the respondent no.1-Indresh Maurya.
2. The present petition calls in question the correctness of
the order dated 25-05-2026 in Criminal Misc.Bail Application
No. 12359/2025 passed by the High Court of Judicature at
Allahabad, Lucknow Bench. By the said order, respondent no.1
has been granted bail in connection with FIR No.319/2025
registered with Masauli Police Station, District Barabanki,
Uttar Pradesh, for the offences punishable under Sections
103(1),  351(3)  and  238  of  the  Bharatiya  Nyaya  Sanhita,
2023(for short, ‘BNS).
3. The petitioner-complainant before us, is the sister of
deceased Vimlesh Pal. The aforesaid FIR No.319/2025 dated
30.07.2025 was registered against the respondent no.1.
4. On 31.07.2025/01.08.2025 the respondent no.1 who was the
husband of the deceased was arrested. The concerned Trial
Judge  at  Baranbaki,  Uttar  Pradesh,  had  dismissed  the
application for bail on 21.11.2025 and on approaching the High
Court, the High Court had enlarged the respondent no.1 on bail
on 25.05.2026.
5. The  High  Court  has  proceeded  on  the  basis  that  on
20.05.2026, when the matter came up before the High Court, the
High Court had asked the Government’s counsel to produce the

--- Page 45 ---
3
general diary to confirm whether the deceased was on duty on
27th, 28th and 29th July 2025 or not? The learned A.G.A.appears
and produce the general diary, in which it was shown that the
deceased was on duty on 27 th, 28th and 29 th July 2025. On the
basis of that, learned counsel for respondent no.1 before the
High Court submitted that there might be the dead body of some
other person, which may have been connected with the present
case and the respondent no.1 has been wrongly made an accused
in the case.
6. After considering the submissions and relying upon the
general diary produced by the Government advocate which showed
that the deceased was on duty on  27 th, 28th and 29th July 2025
and after noticing that the postmortem report estimated the
date of death as 3 to 4 days prior to the date of postmortem
i.e. 30.07.2025. The High Court recorded the following in
paragraph 11 of the impugned order:-
“11.  Considering  the  submissions  made  by  learned
counsel for the parties and going through the record of
the case, prima facie, it is found from the record, as
well as from the General Diary produced by learned
A.G.A, that the sister of the informant was on duty on
27th, 28th and 29th July 2025. As per the post-mortem
report, the date of death has been shown as 3-4 days
prior to the date of post-mortem, i.e., 30.07.2025.
From the record it also appears that during those 3-4
days, the sister of the informant was on duty. Hence,
it appears that the body of some other person has been
connected with the present case. Thus, this this court
is of the view that the applicant has made out a case
for grant of bail.”

--- Page 46 ---
4
7. Learned counsel for the petitioner-complainant (sister of
the deceased) submits that the High Court has overlooked the
fact  that  the  deceased  had  died  on  approximately  around
27.07.2025 and that inquiry had found that there was wrong
entry in the general diary. Learned counsel prayed for setting
aside the impugned order whereby granting bail to respondent
no.1.
8. When the matter came up for hearing on previous occasion
i.e. on 30.09.2026, we directed the learned counsel for the
State to produce the inquiry report. Learned counsel for the
State  has  placed  on  record  the  report,  the  thorough
preliminary report as well as the three orders by which the
penalty of censure were imposed on the three members/employees
of the police department. It must be pointed out here that the
deceased as well as respondent no.1 are members/employees of
the police force/department and the three members/employees
who stand censured were also working in the police department.
9. We have perused the report, the thorough preliminary
report as well as the order of the disciplinary proceedings.
The report is dated 02.08.2025 which is the first annexure (R-
2/1) to the additional affidavit in IA No.309979/2026. This
report was, by the  Circle Officer, Haidergarh, Barabanki ,
Uttar Pradesh, given barely three days after the discovery of
the  body  of  the  deceased.  The  said  report  is  set  out
hereunder:-
“…….It is respectfully submitted that upon my perusal of

--- Page 47 ---
5
the General Diary of Police Station Subeha, District
Barabanki,  it  was  found  that  on  27.07.2025,  Head
Moharrir Prem Prakash Yadav, vide Report No. 41 at 16:14
hrs, recorded the departure of W/C Vimlesh Pal for
Mahadeva  Mela  duty  at  Police  Station  Ramnagar.
Thereafter, on 28.07.2025, Head Moharrir Prem Chandra
Saroj, vide Report No. 28 at 15:01 hrs, recorded the
arrival of the aforementioned W/C Vimlesh Pal from the
Mahadeva Mela law and order duty. On the same day,
28.07.2025,  Head  Moharrir  Prem  Prakash  Yadav,  vide
Report No. 36 at 17:58 hrs, recorded the departure of
W/C Vimlesh Pal for Majitha Mela duty to Police Station
Satrikh, District Barabanki. Furthermore, on 29.07.2025,
Head Moharrir Prem Prakash Yadav, vide Report No. 26 at
12:56 hrs, recorded the arrival of W/C Vimlesh Pal from
the Majitha Mela. Whereas, the dead body of the said W/C
Vimlesh  Pal  was  found  on  30.07.2025  within  the
jurisdiction  of  Police  Station  Masauli,  District
Barabanki. It has been proved that she was murdered on
27.07.2025.This proves that Head Constable Prem Prakash
Yadav and Head Constable Prem Chandra Saroj recorded the
arrival and departure of the said W/C Vimlesh Pal
despite her not being physically present at the police
station.  This  exhibits  gross  negligence  and
arbitrariness on the part of Head Constable Prem Prakash
Yadav and Head Constable Prem Chandra Saroj, as well as
lax supervision by Shri Krishna Kant Singh, Inspector
In-Charge Subeha.
Therefore, this report is respectfully forwarded to you
for necessary action regarding the lax supervision by
Shri Krishna Kant SinghInspector In-Charge Subeha and
the negligent, wrongful recording of the arrival and
departure of the deceased W/C Vimlesh Pal by Head
Constable Prem Prakash Yadav and Head Constable Prem
Chandra Saroj.”

--- Page 48 ---
6
10. Thereafter,  a  detailed  report  dated  27.05.2026  was
submitted  by  the  Circle  Officer,  Sadar,  Barabanki,  Uttar
Pradesh. No doubt this report is two days after the High Court
pronounced the impugned order and the High Court did not have
the benefit of this report. The report dated 02.08.2025 though
available, was not placed by the prosecution before the High
Court.
11. In  the  detailed  inquiry  report,  the  conclusion  is
recorded as under:-
“Conclusion: In the referred matter, upon perusal of the
recorded statements of the concerned personnel and the
was  ascertained  that  the  documentary  records,  it
departure of Lady Constable (CP) Vimlesh Pal, PS Subeha,
District Barabanki for peace and law and order duty at
PS Ramnagar Mahadeva Mela on 27.07.2025 was recorded by
Constable (CP) Mohit Kumar on the ID of HC (CP) Prem
Prakash  Yadav  vide  GD  No.  46  at  17:27  hrs.  On
28.07.2025, on the ID of HC (CP) Prem Prakash Yadav, PS
Subeha, Barabanki, the arrival of Lady Constable Vimlesh
Pal after completion of Mahadeva Mela peace and law and
order duty was recorded by Constable (CP) Mohit Kumar
vide GD No. 38 at 15:01 hrs. On 28.07.2025, on the ID of
HC (CP) Prem Prakash Yadav, PS Subeha, Constable (CP)
Mohit Kumar recorded her departure for peace and law and
order duty at Mela Manjitha, PS Satrikh, Barabanki vide
GD No. 36 at 17:58 hrs. On 29.07.2025 at 12:56 hrs, on
the ID of HC (CP) Prem Prakash Yadav, PS Subeha,
Barabanki, Constable (CP) Mohit Kumar of PS Subeha,
District Barabanki recorded her arrival vide GD No. 26
at  12:56  hrs.  The  departure  for  and  arrival  from
Mahadeva and Manjitha Melas for peace and law and order

--- Page 49 ---
7
duty ought to have been executed by HC (CP) Prem Prakash
Yadav and Constable (CP) Mohit Kumar after physically
verifying Lady Constable Vimlesh Pal at PS Subeha and
establishing telephone contact, yet this was not done by
HC (CP) Prem Prakash Yadav and Constable (CP) Mohit
Kumar, PS Subeha. No inquiry was initiated by the said
personnel regarding Lady Constable (CP) Vimlesh Pal and
no reference was made while recording the night count GD
Entry, nor was any report forwarded regarding the Lady
the  police  station  Constable's  non-appearance
premises/office  whereas  directives  are  periodically
issued by higher officials during inspections of police
stations  stipulating  that  no  arrival  or  departure
entries shall be recorded without the physical presence
of the personnel at the police station. The departure
and arrival of Lady Constable (CP) Vimlesh Pal, PS
Subeha, Barabanki were recorded by Head Moharrir Prem
Prakash Yadav and Constable (CP) Mohit Kumar posted at
the  police  station  office  without  her  ever  being
physically present at the PS Subeha office. Inspector
Shri Krishnakant Singh, Inspector-in-Charge, PS Subeha,
District Barabanki had departed from PS Subeha with the
police contingent on 28.07.2025 for peace arrangement
duty  at  Manjitha  Mela,  Satrikh.  Inspector  Shri
Krishnakant Singh, Inspector-in-Charge Subeha, Barabanki
ought to have conducted physical verification of the
presence  of  all  Head  Constables/Constables/Lady
Constables arriving from PS Subeha at Manjitha Mela, PS
Satrikh during the said duty to definitively ascertain
whether they had reported for duty from PS Subeha or not
but  Inspector  Shri  Krishnakant  Singh,  Inspector-in-
Charge,  PS  Subeha,  District  Barabanki  neglected  to
verify  the  police  personnel  (Head
Constables/Constables/Lady Constables) assigned from PS
Subeha at Manjitha Mela, PS Satrikh, Barabanki which

--- Page 50 ---
8
reflects  the  lax  supervision  of  Inspector  Shri
Krishnakant Singh, the then Inspector-in-Charge Subeha,
presently Inspector-in-Charge PS Kursi, Barabanki. Owing
to  his  lax  supervision,  the  arrival  and  departure
entries of Lady Constable Vimlesh Pal continued to be
made without her reporting to the police station/duty
venue. The culpability of lax supervision is reflected
upon Shri Krishnakant Singh, the then Inspector-in-
Charge PS Subeha / presently Inspector-in-Charge PS
Kursi,  District  Barabanki  and  the  culpability  of
exercising negligence and arbitrariness toward official
obligations is reflected upon HC (CP) Prem Prakash Yadav
(PNO-990895684) and Constable (CP) Mohit Kumar (PNO-
192110583) appointed at PS Subeha, District Barabanki.”
12. Thereafter,  show  cause  notices  were  issued  to  the
members/employees concerned and each of them were censured and
the order of censure was directed to be placed on record in
the service record/character roll of the members/employees
concerned.
13. As is clear from what is stated here and above, though
the report dated 02.08.2025 was available, the same was not
placed before the High Court. The High Court proceeded on the
basis that the deceased was on duty 27th, 28th and 29th July 2025
and  found  a  contradiction  between  the  conclusion  in  the
postmortem report of 30.07.2026 which estimated the death of
the deceased to 3 to 4 days before the date of postmortem and
the assumed fact of the deceased being on duty on  27 th, 28th
and 29th July 2025.
14. In the teeth of the reports that are available, it is

--- Page 51 ---
9
only fair and proper that the High Court has a fresh look in
the matter.
15. Accordingly,  we  set  aside  the  impugned  order  dated
25.05.2026  and  remit  the  Criminal  Misc.Bail  Application
No.12359/2025  to  the  file  of  the  High  Court  for  fresh
consideration in accordance with law.
16. Respondent no.1, who is on bail since 25.05.2026, shall
surrender before the concerned Court on or before 02.11.2026.
17. Needless to say that any observations made in the present
order,  will  not  come  in  the  way  of  the  High  Court  in
independently  considering  the  application  for  bail  of
respondent no.1. The High Court may dispose of the matter in
accordance with law.
18. The Special Leave Petition is disposed of in the above
terms.
19. Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand disposed
of.

CHANDRA SEKHAR KUSUMA

KUSUMA HARI KUMAR             ...APPELLANT(S)

THE STATE OF ANDHRA 
PRADESH & ANR.      ...RESPONDENT(S) 
 
WITH 
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO(S).            OF 2026 
(ARISING OUT OF SLP (CRL.) NO. 3105 OF 2024) 
AND 
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO(S).            OF 2026 
(ARISING OUT OF SLP (CRL.) NO. 6240 OF 2024) 
 
O R D E R 
 
1. Leave granted. 
2. These appeals arise from the final judgment and order 
dated 22nd December, 2023, passed by the High Court 
of Andhra Pradesh at Amaravati in Criminal Petition 
Nos. 2030 of 2021 and 783 of 2022, whereby the High 
Court declined to quash the criminal proceedings arising 
out of Crime No. 18 of 2019, registered on the complaint 
lodged by the respondent -wife against the appellants. 
The appellants in SLP (Crl.) Nos. 2212 of 2024 and 3105 

--- Page 71 ---
2 
 
of 2024 are the sisters of the appellant -husband, 
whereas the appellant in SLP (Crl.) No. 6240 of 2024 is 
the husband himself. 
3. The brief facts necessary for adjudication of the present 
appeals are as follows: 
i. The marriage between the appellant -husband and the 
respondent-wife was solemnised on 24th August, 2018, 
in accordance with Hindu rites and customs. 
ii. The respondent -wife alleged that she was subjected to 
dowry demands and harassment and was assaulted by 
the appellant-husband and his family members on 10th 
March, 2019. The parties have been residing separately 
since 13th March, 2019. 
iii. On 12th March,  2019, the respondent -wife lodged a 
complaint at the Women Police Station, Nellore, pursuant 
to which FIR No. 18 of 2019 was registered for offences 
punishable under Sections 498 -A and 307 read with 
Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860, and Sections 
3 and 4 of the The Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961. Upon 
completion of the investigation, a charge -sheet was filed 
against the accused and registered as PRC No.130/2019. 
iv. The appellant -husband and his father filed Criminal 
Petition No. 783 of 2022, while the appellant -husband’s 
sisters filed Criminal Petition No. 2030 of 2021 before the 
High Court, seeking quashing of the proceedings in P.R.C. 
No. 130 of 2019. 
4. By the impugned judgment and order dated 22nd 
December, 2023, the High Court dismissed both 

--- Page 72 ---
3 
 
petitions, holding that the allegations in the complaint, 
the statements recorded during investigation, the 
charge-sheet and the material on record warranted a 
trial. Accordingly, the High Court declined to quash the 
criminal proceedings at that stage. 
5. We have heard learned counsel for the parties and 
perused the material available on record.  
6. By order dated 16th April, 2024, this Court referred the 
parties to the Supreme Court Mediation Centre to 
explore the possibility of an amicable settlement. 
Pursuant thereto, the parties participated in mediation 
proceedings and arrived at a Settlement Agr eement 
dated 17th May, 2024. 
7. The parties have filed a joint application, being I.A. No. 
307339 of 2026, invoking the jurisdiction of this Court 
under Article 142 of the Constitution of India. By the 
said application, they have placed the Settlement 
Agreement on record and seek dissolu tion of their 
marriage by mutual consent, quashing of the pending 
civil and criminal proceedings arising out of their 
matrimonial dispute, and appropriate directions to 
ensure that no further proceedings are initiated in 
relation thereto. 
8. We have perused the Settlement Agreement and 
interacted with the parties. They have affirmed that the 
settlement has been arrived at voluntarily, of their own 
free will and without any coercion, undue influence or 
fraud. They have further stated that there  is no 

--- Page 73 ---
4 
 
possibility of reconciliation and have expressed their 
unequivocal consent to dissolution of their marriage. 
9. The salient terms of the Settlement Agreement are as 
follows: 
i. The parties have agreed to dissolve their marriage by 
mutual consent by invoking the jurisdiction of this Court 
under Article 142 of the Constitution of India, there being 
no possibility of reconciliation. 
ii. The appellant -husband agreed to pay a sum of 
₹1,52,00,000/- (Rupees One Crore Fifty-Two Lakhs only) 
to the respondent-wife, along with 1 kg of 22 -carat gold 
or 24 -carat gold of equivalent value, in full and final 
settlement of her claims towards alimony, past, present 
and future maintenance, stridhan , belongings and all 
other claims arising out of the matrimonial relationship. 
iii. The cash component of ₹1,52,00,000/- has been paid by 
the appellant-husband and received by the respondent -
wife. In respect of the gold, this Court, by order dated 
13th April, 2026, fixed its value at ₹1,25,00,000/- 
(Rupees One Crore Twenty -Five Lakhs only). The 
respondent-wife has acknowledged receipt of the demand 
draft for ₹50,00,000/- and, pursuant to subsequent 
orders of this Court, a demand draft for the balance 
amount of ₹75,00,000/- has been drawn in her favour. 
iv. The parties have agreed to seek quashing or withdrawal 
of all pending civil and criminal proceedings arising out 
of their matrimonial dispute, as detailed in the Settlement 
Agreement, upon fulfilment of its terms. 

--- Page 74 ---
5 
 
v. The parties have undertaken not to initiate any further 
legal proceedings or complaints against each other or 
their respective family members in relation to the 
matrimonial dispute 
10. The appellant -husband has produced the original 
demand draft for a sum of ₹75,00,000/-, the receipt of 
which has been duly acknowledged by the respondent -
wife. Further, in terms of Clause 9 of the Settlement 
Agreement, the respondent-wife had agreed to furnish a 
No-Objection Certificate (NOC) in favour of Manappuram 
Finance, BTM Layout, Bengaluru, and the appellant -
husband for the release of the ornaments pledged in the 
latter’s name. The said NOC has also been handed over 
to the appellant-husband. 
11. Having considered the terms of the Settlement 
Agreement and interact ion with the parties, we are 
satisfied that the settlement has been arrived at 
voluntarily and that the parties have amicably resolved 
their matrimonial disputes. In the facts and 
circumstances of the case, we are of the considered view 
that this is a fit cas e for exercise of the plenary powers 
of this Court under Article 142 of the Constitution of 
India to do complete justice between the parties and 
bring a quietus to all disputes and proceedings arising 
out of their matrimonial relationship. 
12. We place on record our appreciation for the 
commendable efforts of Mr.Gopal Prasad, learned 
mediator at the Supreme Court Mediation Centre, whose 

--- Page 75 ---
6 
 
sincere and effective efforts facilitated the amicable 
resolution of the disputes between the parties.  
13. Accordingly, I.A. No. 307339 of 2026 is allowed. In view 
of the Settlement Agreement and in exercise of our 
powers under Article 142 of the Constitution of India, we 
pass the following directions: 
13.1. The marriage solemnised  between the appellant -
husband, Chandra Sekhar Pavan Kumar, and the 
respondent-wife, Vaddi Priyanka, on 24th August, 
2018, stands dissolved by a decree of divorce by mutual 
consent. 
13.2.  All pending civil and criminal proceedings instituted by 
either party against the other, or against the members 
of their respective families, arising out of the 
matrimonial dispute, shall stand quashed and shall be 
deemed to have been finally disposed of. These include: 
i. SLP (Crl) No. 2212 of 2024, Chandra Sekhar Kusuma 
Hari Kumar @ Kusuma Hari Kumar vs The State of 
Andhra Pradesh & Anr.

& Anr.

iv. M.C. No. 46 of 2019, Vaddi Priyanka Vs. Pavan Kumar 
Chandrasekhar, Family Court, Nellore, Andhra 
Pradesh.

vi. FIR No. 215 of 2023 dated 03.10.2023, Chinna Bazar

viii. PRC No.130 of 20 19, Judicial First -Class Magistrate-

xxiv. Any other pending civil/criminal proceedings/

14. The parties have affirmed that they shall abide by the 
terms and conditions of the Settlement Agreement and 
shall not initiate any further civil or criminal proceedings

15. The present appeals stand disposed of in the aforesaid

1. We have heard learned counsel appearing for the parties. 
2. I.A. Nos. 263918/2026, 264175/2026 and 264180/2026 
have been filed by the petitioner ’s brothers, namely, 
Dhirendra Singh Baghel, Mrigendra Singh Baghel and 
Ranvijay Singh Baghel, seeking impleadment as party 
petitioners in the present proceedings. The applicants state 
that they were also directors of Sai Prakash Properties 
Development Limited (SPPDL) and have been arrayed as 
accused in certain FIRs arising out of the alleged activities 
of the company. They submit that the present proceedings, 
which concern multiple criminal cases and the settlement 
of investors ’claims, have a bearing on their interests and, 

--- Page 88 ---
W.P.(CRL.) NO.125/2026  2 
 
therefore, seek to be impleaded as parties to the present 
proceedings. 
3. I.A. Nos. 2639 24/2026, 263927/2026 and 264178/2026 
have been filed by the applicants seeking protection 
against coercive action in connection with the aforesaid 
FIRs and the consequential proceedings. 
4. Having regard to the nature of the reliefs sought in the 
aforesaid applications, issue notice to the respondents on 
all the applications. 
5. In the meantime, as an interim measure, no coercive steps 
shall be taken against the applicants in I.A. Nos. 
263924/2026, 263927/2026 and 264178/2026 in 
connection with the FIRs referred to in the respective 
applications and the consequential proceedings, until 
further orders of this Court. 
6. We may now advert to the interim status report submitted 
by the Special Committee constituted by this Court in the 
present proceedings. 
7. Pursuant to the order dated 29th May, 2026, this Court 
constituted a Special Committee headed by Mr. Justice 
Manindra Mohan Shrivastava to settle investors  ’ claims 
and resolve disputes arising from the affairs of Sai Prakash 
Assurance Services Private Limited and its associate 
companies. 

--- Page 89 ---
W.P.(CRL.) NO.125/2026  3 
 
8. Subsequently, by order dated 21.09.2026, this Court, 
upon being informed by learned senior counsel appearing 
for the petitioner that a sale deed had been executed and 
the entire sale consideration had been deposited in the 
escrow account maintained by the Special Committee, 
observed that no corresponding report had been received 
from the Committee. The Committee was, accordingly, 
requested to submit an updated status report within two 
weeks. 
9. The interim status report submitted by the Special 
Committee has been brought on record and perused by us. 
The report details the steps taken by the Committee in 
furtherance of its mandate, the progress made towards the 
verification and settlement of inves tors ’ claims, and the 
further directions sought to facilitate the completion of its 
work. Learned senior counsel appearing for the petitioners 
has also placed before us a compilation of the orders 
passed by the Committee in the course of its proceedings, 
which has also been perused. 
10. The Special Committee has sought directions for the 
appointment of Nodal Officers by the Chief Secretaries of 
Uttarakhand, Madhya Pradesh and Maharashtra, transfer 
of funds lying in 52 frozen bank accounts, furnishing of 
details of investors awaiting refunds, and de-attachment of 
properties belonging to the petitioner, his family members 
and the companies concerned. 

--- Page 90 ---
W.P.(CRL.) NO.125/2026  4 
 
11. Mr. Amarjit Singh Bedi, learned counsel appearing for the 
Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI), informs us 
that SEBI has transferred a sum of ₹37,25,000/- to the 
escrow account maintained in the name of the Special 
Committee. 
12. Learned counsel further submits that 46 bank accounts, 
which have been frozen at the instance of SEBI, contain an 
aggregate amount of ₹1,01,00,000/-. However, according 
to the instructions received by him, there may be liens over 
the said accounts at the instance of other agencies, 
including the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) or the 
local police. SEBI, therefore, requires clarifica tion 
regarding the status of these accounts and the nature of 
any such liens or restrictions before the matter can be 
taken forward. 
13. In our view, the appropriate course for SEBI would be to 
communicate to the Special Committee the complete 
status of the matter, including the particulars of the frozen 
bank accounts, the amounts lying therein and any 
difficulties arising on account of liens or restrictions, if any, 
imposed by other investigating agencies or authorities. The 
Special Committee shall consider the information so 
furnished and take such steps as may be necessary in 
furtherance of the mandate entrusted to it by this Court. 
In th e event any clarification or further directions are 

--- Page 91 ---
W.P.(CRL.) NO.125/2026  5 
 
required in this regard, the Special Committee shall be at 
liberty to apprise this Court. 
14. The Registry shall furnish a copy of the interim status 
report submitted by the Special Committee to learned 
counsel appearing for the parties. 
15. Pursuant to the directions contained in the order dated 
29th May, 2026, the States in which the FIRs have been 
registered or the lands are situated were required to 
appoint Nodal Officers to assist the Special Committee. 
However, the Committee’s report indicates that the States 
of Uttarakhand, Madhya Pradesh and Maharashtra have 
not appointed Nodal Officers despite reminders having 
been issued. 
16. Accordingly, the Chief Secretaries of the aforesaid three 
States are directed to ensure that the Nodal Officers are 
appointed within a period of two weeks from today. In the 
event of non-compliance, this Court may be constrained to 
pass appropriate coerciv e orders against the concerned 
authorities. 
17. The Registry shall also furnish a copy of this order to the 
learned Standing Counsel appearing for the aforesaid 
States.

1. Leave granted.
2. This appeal is directed against an interim order passed by the Delhi High
Court in W.P.(C) No. 4582/2003, whereby the Appellant’s prayer for extension of time
was rejected.
3. The High Court has, inter alia, declined to interfere with the timeline due to the

connected cases.
4. At this stage, we are faced with two key developments:

No. 4582/2003 has also since been disposed of by the Delhi High Court vide
order dated 26.09.2011. It, thus, seems to us that the Appellant’s prayer made

forming the subject matter of this appeal now stand transferred to the High
Court. Now, the foundation of the High Court’s observations, namely, that the
clarification must be sought from this Court, no longer exists.

of this Appeal as infructuous. The questions of law, if any, raised in this case shall
remain open.

passed by the High Court of Madhya Pradesh at Jabalpur
(briefly the ‘High Court’ hereinafter), rejecting the
1

--- Page 104 ---
regular bail application of the appellant.
4. Appellant  is  an  accused  in  Crime  No.244/2025
registered at Police Station- Amarpatan, District- Maihar,
Madhya  Pradesh  under  Sections  8,  21  and  22  of  the
Narcotics Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985 (for
short, ‘NDPS Act’) read with Sections 6/13 of Madhya
Pradesh Drugs (Control) Act, 1959.
5. According to the prosecution, acting on confidential
information, police carried out a raid on a vehicle on
05.05.2025 and recovered 720 bottles (each bottle weighing
100  ml)  of  Onerex  cough  syrup  containing  codeine
phosphate. Appellant and two others, who were in that
vehicle, were arrested.

7. This  Court  had  issued  notice  vide  order  dated
31.08.2026.

respondent-State  of  Madhya  Pradesh  submits  that  on
completion of investigation, charge-sheet was submitted
before the Special Court. Charges were framed in December,
2025.
9. Learned counsel for the appellant submits that as of
today,  one  witness  is  being  examined.  There  are  13
prosecution witnesses in total.
10. Considering the above, we are of the view that the
benefit of bail may be extended to the appellant.
11. That being the position, t he impugned order dated
2

--- Page 105 ---
21.07.2026 passed by the High Court is set aside.
12. Consequently, we direct that the appellant Prateek
Singh shall be produced before the jurisdictional Special
Court within a maximum period of 07 days from today,
whereafter he shall be released on bail on such terms and
conditions as may be deemed appropriate. Appellant shall
co-operate  with  the  trial  and  not  seek  unnecessary
adjournments.
13. Accordingly, the Criminal Appeal is allowed.
14. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.

3

information, police carried out a raid on a vehicle on

registered prior to registration of the present case.

benefit of bail may be extended to the appellant.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL  NO.12977/2025
GIRIJAKANTA ROUT                                   APPELLANT(S)
                                VERSUS
ORISSA ADMINISTRATIVE TRIBUNAL & ORS.              RESPONDENT(S)
WITH
C.A. No. 12979/2025
C.A. No. 12978/2025
O R D E R
1. We have heard the learned counsel appearing for the
appellants and the respondents. 
2. The private appellant(s) before us were duly appointed as
Live Stock Inspectors, pursuant to an advertisement dated
16.01.2004 issued by The Director, Veterinary and Animal
Husbandry,  Odisha.  In  an  earlier  notification  dated
07.01.2000 issued by the Government of Orissa, Fisheries
and A.R.D Department, the Selection Committee for the
said post had been constituted in which the Project
Director, DRDA was not notified as a member. However, by
the subsequent notification issued by the Government of
Orissa dated 28.11.2003, the said authority was also made
a member of the Selection Committee. 

--- Page 111 ---
2
3. Pursuant to the aforesaid advertisement, 45 candidates
were called for interview on 22.06.2004 and selection has
been made in the year 2006 by the subsequent Selection
Committee, after which the appellants and the other
candidates joined in the training and were appointed in
the year 2008. Thereafter, they have been duly serving in
the capacity of Live Stock Inspectors for the past 18
years. 
4. In the year 2006, challenges have been made to the
aforestated  appointments  by  candidates  who  were  not
selected or appointed. The Orissa Administrative Tribunal
was pleased to dismiss the said challenges in the year
2011. After the decision of the Orissa Administrative
Tribunal, strangely, a suo motu proceeding was initiated
by the Additional Secretary to the Government of Orissa,
Department of Fisheries and ARD Department, Bhubaneswar
and it was, accordingly, found that due procedure had not
been followed in the selection of candidates to the post
of Live Stock Inspector and, hence, it was recommended to
declare the selection as null and void. This was done on
the premise that the Project Director, DRDA was a Member
of the Selection Committee. On 27.06.2012, the private
appellant(s) and 11 others were terminated from service
with immediate effect. The original application and the
writ petition filed by the private appellant(s) before
us, challenging their termination, were dismissed by the

--- Page 112 ---
3
Tribunal and the High Court, respectively, and the order
of termination was upheld. Consequently, a direction to
prepare a fresh selection list was issued.
5. Now, not only the private appellant(s), but the State has
also challenged the said decision of the High Court
before us, by taking a  u-turn and seek to support  the
private appellant(s), probably, on the premise that the
private appellant(s) are not at fault and, in any case,
they have been in continuous service for the past 18
years.
6. The  learned  counsel  appearing  for  the  private
appellant(s) would submit that it is nobody's case that
the  private  appellant(s)  were  responsible  for  the
procedural violation qua the Selection Committee. In any
case, such a violation,  ipso facto,  will not make or
render the selection bad in law.
7. It is further submitted that the private respondent(s)
before us also would not be a beneficiary, since the
order under challenge only facilitates a fresh selection.
Furthermore, the private respondent(s) also participated
in the selection process and they did not get selected.
8. Learned counsel appearing for the private respondent(s)
would submit that since the selection was contrary to
law, there is no need to interfere with the impugned
order of the High Court, confirming that of the Tribunal.
9. Upon  hearing  the  learned  counsel  appearing  for  the

--- Page 113 ---
4
respective parties, we hold that both the Tribunal and
the High Court have committed a serious error. The
principle  of  natural  justice  has  got  two  different
facets. The first facet would be one which has the effect
of making the very decision void ab initio, on the face
of it. The other facet is one pertaining to procedural
violation which would only make the decision voidable. 
10. In the case at hand, both the private appellant(s) and
the  private  respondent(s)  have  participated  in  the
selection  process.  In  other  words,  had  the  private
respondent(s) been selected, they would have also gone to
the other side, by supporting the case of the private
appellant(s). The private appellant(s) have continued in
service for the past 18 years. It is absolutely not their
fault for the so called procedural violation in the
Constitution of the Selection Committee.  Admittedly, it
is  the  Government,  by  way  of  notification,  which
constituted the Selection Committee. 
11. Taking note of the above observations and reasons, we set
aside the impugned judgment of the High Court confirming
that of the Tribunal. The private appellant(s) are held
entitled to continue with their service and the direction
to the State authorities to prepare a fresh selection
list stands quashed. Needless to state that the order of
the Tribunal also stands set aside. 
12. The appeals stand allowed, accordingly.

--- Page 114 ---
5
13. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NO(S).  3298/2012
B. RAGHAVENDRA HEDGE (D) BY LRS.                   APPELLANT(S)
                                VERSUS
MANORAMA J.SHANBHOGUE(D) BY LRS. & ORS.            RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1.  We have heard the learned Senior Counsel appearing for the
appellant and the respondent(s).
2. Respondent No. 01-Plaintiff filed a suit for partition.
Aggrieved by the preliminary decree passed by the Trial Court
as confirmed by the High Court, the present appeal is filed
by Defendant No. 2, who is the appellant herein.  Both the
Courts have held that all the suit properties are joint
family properties. 
3. There are three schedules of properties before us. Schedule A
has five items. Item No.1 is a property in which the
partnership firm, which is the subject matter of Scheduled
‘C’ property, is situated. It is the case of the respondents
that the said property is a joint family property, while the

--- Page 118 ---
2
learned  Senior  Counsel  appearing  for  the  appellant(s)
contends that the property belongs to the Temple and he is
the tenant. He submits that it was initially taken on rent by
his father, who returned it. Item Nos. 2, 3, and 5 are
immovable properties. Item 4 has not been put into partition
even by both the Courts. 
4. The Schedule ‘B’ properties consist of movables, and the
Schedule ‘C’ property is the business of “Hegde Medicals”
being carried on the premises of the property listed under
item no.1 of Schedule A. Both the Courts have found that all
the properties are joint family properties. 
5. Learned Senior Counsel appearing for the appellant would
submit that the application filed by him, invoking Order 41
Rule 27 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1973 (for short, the
CPC), has not been disposed of while disposing of the appeal.
He contends that adequate evidence is available in the
documents filed to show that the ‘C’ Schedule property, i.e.,
the  business  of  “Hegde  Medicals”,  is  not  joint  family
property and Item No.1 of the Scheduled ‘A’ properties is one
in which the appellant(s) is a tenant and, therefore, is also
not a joint family property. 
6. Incidentally, it is submitted that as much as Item No.2 of
‘A’ Schedule is a house property, the appellant(s) shall be
given the benefit of Section 32 of the Hindu Succession Act,
1956 (for short, the Act, 1956) read with Section 24 of the

--- Page 119 ---
3
Partition Act, 1893 (for short, the Act, 1983).
7. The learned Senior Counsel appearing for the respondents
would submit that factual findings have been given by both
the Courts on the nature of the properties concerned.  He
further submits that Section 22 of the Act, 1956 read with
Section 24 of the Act, 1893 cannot be pressed into service in
the present proceedings. In such view of the matter, he
contends that there is no need for any interference.
8. We are inclined to remit the matter back to the High Court
only insofar as ‘C’ Schedule property and Item No.1 of the
‘A’ Scheduled property alone are concerned. 
9. Touching upon these properties, the appellant has filed an
application seeking production of additional documents by
invoking Order 41 Rule 27 of the CPC. This Court has
reiterated time and again regarding the ambit of Order 41 and
Rule 27, and therefore there is no need to delve into the
same. Similarly, we do not want to express anything on the
admissibility,  relevancy  and  proof  of  the  additional
documents that are sought to be produced. 
10. Suffice it is to state that the High Court was duty bound to
consider the application at the time of disposing of the
appeal; unfortunately, the same has not been done. 
11. In such view of the matter, we are inclined to set aside the
judgment and decree of the High Court insofar as Item No.1 of
‘A’ Schedule Property and the ‘C’ Schedule Property and remit

--- Page 120 ---
4
it back. All the issues pertaining to those properties are
left open, including admissibility, relevancy and proof of
the documents sought to be marked.
12. Insofar as properties other than Item No.1 of ‘A’ Schedule
Property and the ‘C’ Schedule Property are concerned, we are
inclined to hold that the law is quite settled that whenever
the property stands in the name of the karta, the same is
presumed to be a joint family property and, therefore, the
onus to prove otherwise is on the person who repudiates the
claim of joint family property. In the absence of any
evidence to that effect and in view of the settled decisions,
we  are  confirming  the  decision  rendered  on  the  other
properties.
13. The judgment and decree of the Trial Court as confirmed by
the High Court insofar as Item No.1 of ‘A’ Schedule Property
and the ‘C’ Schedule Property stand set aside, and the matter
is remitted back to the High Court for fresh consideration to
that extent. In respect of other properties, the judgment and
decree of the Trial Court as confirmed by the High Court is
upheld.
14. We request the High Court to make an endeavour to dispose of
the appeal within a period of one year from the date of
receipt of a copy of this order.  
15. Liberty is given to the appellant(s) to raise the plea on
Section 32 of the Act, 1956 read with Section 24 of the Act,

--- Page 121 ---
5
1983, in the manner known to law. 
16. The appeal stands allowed in part, accordingly.
17. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.

Petition(s) for Special Leave to Appeal (Crl.)  No(s).  20544/2026
[Arising out of impugned final judgment and order dated  06-08-2026

MADAN & ANR.                                       Petitioner(s)
                                VERSUS

For Respondent(s) : 
          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
Heard.
2. The petitioners herein, along with five co-accused persons, were
initially arraigned as accused in FIR No. 83 of 1984 dated 12 th June,
1984 registered at the Police Station Dewa, District Barabanki for the
1

--- Page 125 ---
offences punishable under Sections 147, 148, 149 and 302 of the
Indian  Penal  Code,  1860 1.  Upon  conclusion  of  the  investigation,
chargesheet  was  submitted  against  the  accused  persons  for  the
offences punishable under Sections 148, 302/149, and 307/149 of
the IPC.
3. Pursuant  to  the  trial  conducted  in Sessions Trial No. 387 of
1984,  the  learned  II nd Additional  District  and  Sessions  Judge,
Barabanki,2 vide  judgment  and  order  dated  4 th February,  1986,
convicted  and  sentenced  the  petitioners  and  five  co-accused  as
under:-
Section(s) Sentence awarded
Section 302 read with
Section 149 IPC
Imprisonment for life
Section 307 read with
Section 149 IPC
Four years’ rigorous
imprisonment.
Section 148 IPC Further two years rigorous
imprisonment.
All the sentences were ordered to run concurrently.
4. Aggrieved by the judgment of conviction and order of sentence(s)
passed by the trial Court, five out of the seven convicted accused
persons, including the petitioners herein, preferred Criminal Appeal
No. 146 of 1986 before the High Court of Judicature at Allahabad,
Lucknow Bench3.
5. During the pendency of the appeal before the High Court, co-
accused Prabhu and Ram Das passed away, whereupon the appeal
stood abated as against them  vide order dated 19 th February, 2020.
Subsequently, co-accused Sant Ram also passed away, and the appeal
stood abated to his extent  vide  order dated 7 th January, 2026. This
Court  is  informed  that  five  out  of  the  seven  originally  convicted
1  For short, “IPC”. 
2  Hereinafter, referred to as “trial Court”. 
3  Hereinafter, referred to as “High Court”.  
2

--- Page 126 ---
accused passed away during the pendency of the proceedings, thereby
leaving the petitioners herein, Madan and Bharat, as the only two
surviving accused.
6. The High Court, vide judgment and order dated 6th August, 2026,
dismissed Criminal Appeal No. 146 of 1986, affirmed the conviction
and sentences awarded to the petitioners (as mentioned above) and
directed  them  to  surrender  forthwith  to  serve  out  their  remaining
sentence.
7. Aggrieved  by  the  dismissal  of  their  appeal  and  direction  to
surrender, the petitioners have approached this Court by way of the
instant special leave petition. 
8. Shri  Pradeep  Kumar  Yadav  inter  alia advanced  the  following
submissions in order to contend that conviction of the petitioners for
the offences punishable under Sections 148, 302/149, and 307/149
of the IPC is unjustified and unsustainable in the eyes of law: -
i. That  no  independent  witnesses  were  examined  by  the
prosecution in support of its case, even though the incident took place
within the public gaze. 
ii. The case of the prosecution was based primarily on the testimony
of the complainant, Deena Nath (PW-1), and  Krishna Kumar (PW-2) ,
both  of  whom  are  sons  of  the  deceased and,  therefore, interested
witnesses. In absence of corroboration of their testimony by evidence
of any independent witness or incriminating recovery, the conviction of
the petitioners cannot be sustained.
iii. That no weapons were recovered during investigation and hence,
the  ocular  testimony  of  the  closely  related  eye-witnesses  stands
completely uncorroborated.
iv. That no specific role was assigned to the petitioners and hence,
3

--- Page 127 ---
their conviction for the offences punishable under Sections 302/149
and 307/149 of the IPC is unsustainable in facts as well as in law.
9. We have heard and considered the submissions advanced by Shri
Yadav, learned counsel appearing for the petitioners, and have gone
through the impugned judgment and the material placed on record.
10. The deceased Mahattam Dube was working in his field raising an
embankment (mend) alongside his son, Deena Nath (PW-1) 4, at which
point of time the accused persons, including the petitioners, came to
the field. Accused Prabhu, Radhey, and Phool Chand were holding
firearms. Accused Ram Das and Sant Ram were holding country-made
bombs in a bag, and accused Madan and Bharat (petitioners herein)
were armed with lathis and knives.
11. Initially, accused Prabhu, Radhey, and Phool Chand fired shots
at the father of the complainant i.e, the deceased, but he ducked down
and escaped the direct path of the projectiles. The complainant, who
ran to rescue his father, was hit by the firearm pellets. The petitioner-
Madan also hit him on his left hand with a lathi. Accused Ram Das
and Sant Ram hurled country made bombs towards the deceased,
which fell into water and failed to explode.
12. The complainant and his father pleaded for their lives and tried
to run away. However, when they reached near the bushes of the
Ajgana Canal, the petitioner-Madan hit the complainant’s father from
behind with a lathi, and accused Prabhu, Phool Chand, and Radhey
shot at him, causing him to fall. The accused persons then dragged
the complainant’s father onto the bank ( patri) of the canal, where
accused Ram Das and Sant Ram beat him with lathis, and petitioners
Madan and Bharat stabbed him with knives in the abdomen, head,
and neck. The incident was also witnessed by Krishna Kumar (PW-2),
4  Hereinafter, referred to as “complainant”.
4

--- Page 128 ---
son of the deceased, who reached the spot near the place of incident
when the attack was underway.
13. Dr. Prem Prakash (PW-3), who conducted postmortem upon the
body of the deceased, found multiple wounds totaling 23 on the dead
body. These included firearm injuries, contusions, incised wounds,
and stab injuries all over the body.
14. Likewise, when the complainant was medically examined by Dr.
K. Kumar (PW-6), as many as  14 injuries caused by firearm  were
found existing on his person. Hence, it is apparent that the evidence of
the eye-witnesses is thoroughly corroborated by the medical evidence.
15. We have gone through the depositions of Deena Nath (PW-1) and
Krishna Kumar (PW-2) placed on record along with the special leave
petition and find them to be witnesses of sterling worth.
16. The law is well-settled that where the direct testimony of an eye-
witness  is  found  to  be  reliable,  the  same  does  not  require
corroboration in form of any recovery, etc.
17. In an incident of this nature, where a group of accused persons
armed tooth and nail, formed an unlawful assembly, went to the field
of the deceased, and attacked the victims in a brutal manner, the
chance of any independent witness stepping forward to give testimony
against the accused would be negligible.
18. In this background, we find no merit in the submission advanced
by  Mr.  Yadav  that  the  testimony  of  the  eye-witnesses  is  not
corroborated in material particulars or that their testimony cannot be
relied upon in absence of the recovery of weapons.
19. The accused persons were convicted for the offences punishable
under Section 302 and 307 of the IPC with the aid of Section 149 of
the IPC. There is ample evidence on record to show that they formed
5

--- Page 129 ---
an unlawful assembly, armed themselves with multiple weapons and,
upon  reaching  the  place  of  incident,  launched  an  indiscriminate
assault on the deceased as well as the complainant. Thus, there was
no burden upon the prosecution to lead evidence about the individual
role of each accused so as to hold them guilty of the charges. The
accused persons, who were armed tooth and nail, proceeded to the
place of occurrence in form of an unlawful assembly and launched a
brutal assault in furtherance of the common object of the unlawful
assembly. Therefore, the trial Court was fully justified in invoking
Section 149 of the IPC to hold them vicariously liable for the offences
in question.
20. Mr. Yadav made a last-ditch effort by pleading that the accused
persons  are  in  their  late  seventies and  are suffering  from  various
medical ailments and hence, the Court may consider taking a lenient
view on the question of sentence.
21. Suffice it to say that the incident took place in the year 1984 and
the trial was concluded expeditiously within a period of two years. It
was at the appellate stage that the matter got stalled and remained
pending for almost forty years. In any event, an offence punishable
under Section 302 of the IPC, carries a mandatory statutory minimum
sentence of imprisonment for life. Hence, the petitioners, citing their
old age, cannot claim any benefit on the aspect of sentence merely
because significant time has elapsed since the date of incident.
22. It  would,  however,  be  open  to  the  respondent-State  of  Uttar
Pradesh  to  consider  any  prayer  for  remission  submitted  by  the
petitioners, if applicable, in accordance with law at the appropriate
stage.
23. As  an  upshot  of  the  aforesaid  discussion,  we  are  of  the
6

--- Page 130 ---
considered view that the impugned judgments passed by the courts

1. Heard.
2. The  present  petition  arises  out  of  the  order
dated 16th October, 2026 passed by the High Court
of Gujarat at Ahmedabad (hereinafter referred to as
the  “High  Court”)  in  Criminal  Misc.  Application
(Temporary Bail) No.4 of 2026 in Criminal Appeal

was permitted to be released on temporary bail for a
period of one day, from 7:00 a.m. to 7:00 p.m. from
the  date  of  his  actual  release,  to  enable  him  to
attend to his step-brother, who is stated to be in a
critical condition and undergoing treatment at the
New Civil Hospital, Surat. The petitioner, who had
SLP(Crl.)No(s).  20580/2026
2

--- Page 133 ---
sought temporary bail for a period of 30 days, is
aggrieved  by  the  limited  duration  of  interim  bail

3. The petitioner stands convicted for the offences
punishable under Sections 143, 147, 148, 149, 189,
332, 353, 386, 294(b), 506(2), 201 and 34 of the
Indian Penal Code, 1860, and Section 25(1-a) of the
Arms Act, 1959, and has been sentenced to undergo
imprisonment  for  a  period  of  seven  years.  He
preferred Criminal Appeal No.1751 of 2026 before
the High Court, which was admitted on 31 st July,
2026. However, his application seeking suspension
of  sentence  was  rejected  by  the  High  Court  vide
order dated 24th August, 2026.
4. Shri  Kapil  Sibal  and  Shri  Shadan  Farasat,
learned senior counsel appearing for the petitioner,
submitted that the interim bail for a period of one
day  granted  by  the  High  Court  was  absolutely
inadequate, having regard to the critical condition of
the petitioner's step-brother, the distance between
the  jail  and  the  hospital,  and  the  need  to  make
SLP(Crl.)No(s).  20580/2026

--- Page 134 ---
arrangements  for  his  further  treatment  and  the

5. Shri Tushar Mehta, learned Solicitor General

appearing for the respondent no.4 Bank.
3. Our order dated 15.07.2026 reads thus:-
“1. We heard Ms. Meenakshi Arora, the learned senior
counsel appearing for the appellant, Mr. Navin Pahwa, the
learned senior counsel appearing for the respondent no.1
(shareholder), Mr. Rajesh Kumar Gautam, the learned senior

Krishnan Venugopal, the learned senior counsel appearing
for the respondent no.2 and in the last, we also heard Mr.
C.A. Sundaram, the learned senior counsel appearing for a

“A. Admit and the Allow the instant Civil Appeal
