3. Having  regard  to  the  nature  of  the  submissions
canvassed before us, it is difficult for us to adjudicate
the disputed question of fact.
4. The matter is coming up before the NCLAT Principal
Bench, New Delhi on 23.07.2026. It shall be open for all
the concerned to raise all legal contentions available to
them before the NCLAT on 23.07.2026.
5. It shall also be open for the client of Mr. Sundaram
to make his submissions before the NCLAT, if at all, he is
a party before the NCLAT. If the client of Mr. Sundaram is
not a party, he may apply and it is for the NCLAT to
decide whether the client of Mr. Sundaram is a proper or a
necessary party in the proceedings.
6. We make an earnest request to the NCLAT to see that
on 23.07.2026 the matter is heard for sure. We make this
2

--- Page 140 ---
request to the NCLAT because we are informed that NCLT has
reserved the order insofar Section 7 IBC application is
concerned.
7. With the aforesaid, these appeals stand disposed of.
8. Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand
disposed of.”
4. By our order referred to above, we had made an earnest
request to the NCLAT to ensure that the main matter is heard
on 23.07.2026. We made this request to the NCLAT considering
that the NCLT had reserved its order insofar as Section 7
IBC application is concerned.
5. Today, the learned senior counsel appearing for the
applicant brought to our notice that the NCLAT has not heard
the matter till this date. They also brought to our notice
that in the meantime, the order that was reserved by the
NCLT has been pronounced and Section 7 IBC application has
been admitted.
6. We are quite disturbed with the manner in which the
NCLAT has conducted itself in the present litigation. The
request made is out of deference to their position and to
ensure that the judicial office they hold is not belittled
in any manner.
7. When the Supreme Court makes a request to any Court or
Tribunal, it has to be construed as a direction and not just
a request. It is one thing that the Supreme Court earnestly
requests in the hope that the Court or the Tribunal would
abide by the request and do the needful. However, today, we
make it very clear that if there is any request made by the
3

--- Page 141 ---
Supreme Court to any Court or Tribunal, the same shall be
treated as a direction and non-compliance of such direction
shall be looked into very seriously.
8. A similar situation arose where the High Court despite
this Court directing the parties to approach that court for
expeditious consideration and expressing that the High Court
would give due attention to the prayer, the Division Bench
of the High Court recorded an order that having considered
the matter, they find no reason to grant precedence. This
Court in  Spencer and Co., Ltd. and Anr v. Vishwadarshan
Distributors Pvt. Ltd. and ors.  reported in 1995 SCC (1)
259, restrained itself, exercising judicial statesmanship
and held so: 
“6. Ex facie courtesy is the blend of our order of 14-1-
1994. Outwardly it is neither commanding in nature nor
explicitly in terms of a direction. Such is not the sheen
and tone of our order, meant as it was, for a high
constitutional  institution,  being  the  High  Court.  It
comes from another high constitutional institution (this
Court) hierarchically superior in the corrective ladder.
When one superior speaks to another it is always in
language sweet, soft and melodious; more suggestive than
directive. Judicial language is always chaste.
7. Traditions and norms in this regard, well-established
and followed in this country since time immemorial, are
best reflected in the “Song Celestial”, the Bhagavad
Gita. It would for the purpose be apposite to turn to the
18th  Chapter  of  the  Bhagavad  Gita,  containing  the
concluding portion of the dialogue between Lord Krishna,
the Best of Beings, (Purushotamma) and Arjuna, the Best
of Humans, (Narotamma), both superiors in themselves.
Verse 63 in the words of Lord Krishna is:
guhyad guhyataram maya
vimrishayaitad eshneshena
yathecchasi tatha kuru
Translation
Thus I have explained to you the most confidential
4

--- Page 142 ---
of all knowledge. Deliberate on this fully, and
then do what you wish to do.
(emphasis ours)
8. Verse 73 containing the answering words of Arjuna
is:
nashto mohah smritir labdha
tvat prasaddan mayachyuta
sthito'smi gata-sandehah
karishye vachanam tava
 Translation
O infallible one, my illusion is now gone. I have
regained my memory by Your mercy, and I am now firm and
free from doubt and am prepared to act according to
Your instructions. 
(emphasis ours)
For Arjuna, the freedom given to act as he wished to,
was  an  illusion;  acting  in  conformity  with  the
instructions of Krishna a bounden duty. This message
has  perceptibly  percolated  down  as  part  of  Indian
culture, philosophy and behavioural setting the tenor
in the Constitution for interaction between the high
constitutional authorities and institutions. One needs
only  to  be  aware  of  this  thought  with  which  the
Constitution is soaked.
9. Recently, on a lesser aberration, this Court in
Bayer India Ltd. v. State of Maharashtra [(1993) 3 SCC
29] had occasion to strike a sad note in the following
words: (SCC pp. 31-32, paras 5-6)
“5. We are saddened to notice that in spite of the
Court's request contained in this order dated 6-2-
1991, the High Court has not disposed of the review
petition till now. The High Court was requested to
dispose of the said writ petition within four months
from the date of the said order and, at any rate, by
30-9-1991. It is more than two years since the order
was made. While we certainly respect the independence
of the High Court and recognise that it is a co-equal
institution, we cannot but say, at the same time,
that  the  constitutional  scheme  and  judicial
discipline requires that the High Court should give
due regard to the orders of this Court which are
binding on all courts within the territory of India.
The request made in this case was contained in a
judicial  order.  It  does  no  credit  to  either
institution that it has not been heeded to. We hope
and trust that the delay in the disposal of the
review is either accidental or on account of some or
other procedural problem. Be that as it may, the
present situation would not have arisen if only the
review petition had been disposed of within the time
contemplated in the order dated 6-2-1990.
5

--- Page 143 ---
6. In this view of the matter, the IA is disposed of
with the following directions:
(1) We reiterate our request to the High Court to
dispose of the review petition expeditiously, at any
rate within two months of this order.
(2) (3) ***”
The case which we are dealing with is far more angular
because  there  is  a  deliberate  and  conscious
obstruction, put and recorded by the Hon'ble Judges of
the High Court, even when the judicial order of this
Court dated 14-1-1994 was before them, in support of
the prayer for an early durated hearing of the appeal.
The case in hand is of a negative or reverse action,
whereas Bayer India case [(1993) 3 SCC 29] was barely
of inaction, far less in gravity.
10. The afore-narrated words, we think, presently, are
enough to assert the singular constitutional role of
this Court, and correspondingly of the assisting role
of all authorities, civil or judicial, in the territory
of  India,  towards  it,  who  are  mandated  by  the
Constitution to act in aid of this Court. That the High
Court is one such judicial authority covered under
Article 144 of the Constitution is beyond question. The
order  dated  14-1-1994  of  this  Court  was  indeed  a
judicial order and otherwise enforceable throughout the
territory  of  India  under  Article  142  of  the
Constitution. The High Court was bound to come in aid
of this Court when it required the High Court to have
its order worked out. The language of request oftenly
employed by this Court in such situations is to be read
by the High Court as an obligation, in carrying out the
constitutional mandate, maintaining the writ of this
Court running large throughout the country.”
9. Polite expression does not diminish authority, rather
it enhances, which should never be understood as weakness.
10. We are informed that the next date fixed by the NCLAT
is 17.11.2026.
11. Issue notice, returnable on 19.11.2026.
12. Dasti service, in addition, is permitted.
13. The NCLAT shall offer its explanation as to why the
matter has not been heard till this date, despite our
specific order referred to above.
6

--- Page 144 ---
14. In the meantime, there shall not be any constitution of
the CoC.

SONU KUMAR @ SHASHI              ...RESPONDENT(S) 
 
O R D E R 
  
1. The present transfer petition has been filed by the 
petitioner-wife seeking transfer of Matrimonial Case No. 
962 of 2025, instituted by the respondent -husband and 
pending before the Principal Judge, Family Court, Patna, 
Bihar, to the Principal Judge, Famil y Court, 
Jamshedpur, Jharkhand. 
2. The marriage between the parties was solemnised on 
28th November, 2021, in accordance with Hindu rites 
and customs. The parties have been residing separately 
since October, 2023. 
3. The petitioner has instituted Complaint Case No. 1396 of 
2025 and proceedings under Section 125 of the Code of 
Criminal Procedure, 1973, both pending before JMFC, 
Jamshedpur, Jharkhand. The respondent has instituted 

--- Page 158 ---
TP(C.)No.3599 of 2025  2 
 
Matrimonial Case No. 962 of 2025, seeking dissolution of 
marriage, which is pending before the Principal Judge, 
Family Court, Patna, Bihar. 
4. We have heard learned counsel for the parties and 
perused the material placed on record. 
5. During the pendency of the present transfer petition, this 
Court, by order dated 8th April, 2026, referred the 
dispute between the parties to the Supreme Court 
Mediation Centre. Pursuant thereto, the parties arrived 
at a settlement, which was reduced in writing in a 
Settlement Agreement dated 1st June, 2026. 
6. A joint application, being I.A. No. 323101 of 2026, has 
been filed under Article 142 of the Constitution of India, 
seeking appropriate orders to give effect to the Settlement 
Agreement, including dissolution of the marriage and 
closure of all pending proce edings arising out of the 
matrimonial dispute.  
7. We have perused the Settlement Agreement and have 
interacted with the parties. They have affirmed before us 
that the settlement has been arrived  at voluntarily, of 
their own free will and without any coercion, undue 
influence or fraud. They have further stated that there is 

--- Page 159 ---
TP(C.)No.3599 of 2025  3 
 
no possibility of reconciliation and have mutually agreed 
to dissolve their marriage. 
8. Under the terms of the Settlement Agreement, the 
respondent has agreed to pay a sum of ₹27,00,000/- 
(Rupees Twenty -Seven Lakh only) to the petitioner 
towards full and final settlement of all claims arising out 
of their matrimonial relationship. The parties have also 
agreed to seek closure of the pending proceedings arising 
out of the matrimonial dispute and have undertaken not 
to raise any further claims or initiate any civil or criminal 
proceedings against each other in relation thereto. 
9. The respondent has paid the aforesaid amount in two 
instalments. The first instalment of ₹15,00,000/- 
(Rupees Fifteen Lakh only) was credited to the petitioner's 
account on 18th July, 2026, and the second instalment 
of ₹12,00,000/- (Rupees Twelve Lakh only) was paid on 
24th September, 2026. The petitioner has acknowledged 
receipt of the entire settlement amount and confirmed 
that no monetary claims remain outstanding between the 
parties. 
10. We are satisfied that the Settlement Agreement has been 
voluntarily executed by the parties and that its terms are 
lawful. Having regard to the amicable resolution of all 
disputes through mediation before the Supreme Court 

--- Page 160 ---
TP(C.)No.3599 of 2025  4 
 
Mediation Centre and the unequivocal desire of the 
parties to bring their matrimonial relationship to an end, 
we are of the considered view that this is a fit case for 
exercise of the plenary powers of this Court under Article 
142 of the Constitution of In dia to do complete justice 
between the parties and bring a quietus to all disputes 
arising out of their matrimonial relationship. 
11. We place on record our appreciation for the commendable 
efforts of Mr. Sanjeev Kumar, learned Mediator, and the 
co-mediators, Mr. Vikas Bali, Ms. Kakali Roy and Ms. 
Geetanjali Sahni Attri, at the Supreme Court Mediation 
Centre. Their sincere and effective efforts have facilitated 
an amicable resolution of the disputes between the 
parties. 
12. Accordingly, I.A. No. 323101 of 2026 is allowed. In terms 
of the Settlement Agreement which shall form part of this 
order and in exercise of our powers under Article 142 of 
the Constitution of India, we issue the following 
directions: 
12.1. The marriage solemnised between the petitioner 
and the respondent on 28th November, 2021 stands 
dissolved by a decree of divorce by mutual consent. 

--- Page 161 ---
TP(C.)No.3599 of 2025  5

instituted by either party against the other, arising out 
of or in connection with their matrimonial relationship 
or the disputes forming the subject matter of the 
Settlement Agreement, shall stand quashed and 
disposed of in terms of this order. This shall include, 
inter alia: 
(i) OM No.121 of 2024 pending before JMFC, 
Jamshedpur, Jharkhand.  
(ii) CC No.1396 of 2025 pending before JMFC, 
Jamshedpur, Jharkhand  
(iii) Matrimonial Divorce Case No.962 of 2025 pending 
before Principal Judge, Family Court, Patna, Bihar  
12.3. The parties shall abide by the terms and 
conditions of the Settlement Agreement and shall not 
raise any further claims or initiate any civil or criminal 
proceedings against each other in respect of the

WP(Crl.)No.422 of 2026  1 
 
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA 
CRIMINAL ORIGINAL JURISDICTION 
 
WRIT PETITION (CRIMINAL) NO. 422 of 2026 
 
MOHAMMAD JAMAL  
MOHAMMAD YUNUS         ...PETITIONER (S) 
VERSUS  
THE STATE OF  MAHARASHTRA       ...RESPONDENT(S) 
 
 
O R D E R 
 
 
1. The present writ petition under Article 32 of the 
Constitution of India (hereinafter referred to as ‘the 
Constitution’) has been filed by the petitioner, primarily 
seeking a direction for release and return of his licensed 
revolver bearing License No.9040, NPB No. 4571 (Meja) 
which was seized in connection with FIR No. 2 of 2012 
at Bazar Peth Police Station, Jalgaon, Maharashtra. 
The petitioner also seeks appropriate directions for 
expeditious disposal of the proceedings concerning the 
release of the said r evolver which are pending before 
the Bombay High Court.  
2. The facts giving rise to the present writ petition are as 
follows:  

--- Page 164 ---
WP(Crl.)No.422 of 2026  2 
 
2.1. The petitioner is a private bodyguard by 
profession. He was granted an arms license 
bearing License No. 9040, NPB No. 4571. The 
revolver was seized during investigation of FIR 
No. 2 of 2012 under sections 307, 109, 201 read 
with section 34 of the Indian Pe nal Code, 1860 
and sections 3 and 25 of the Arms Act, 1959. 
Petitioner was arrayed as accused No. 8 in the 
said case. It formed a part of the case property in 
Sessions Case No. 192 of 2012.  
2.2. By judgment dated 11.03.2013, the Sessions 
Court acquitted all eight accused of the offences 
charged. It further directed that the items seized 
from the accused be returned after the expiry of 
the appeal period.  
2.3. Petitioner filed an application under section 452 
of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (for 
short, CrPC) dated 14.01.2014 seeking return of 
the revolver. He submitted that he was unable to 
secure employment anywhere without the 
revolver. He further expr essed willingness to 
comply with any conditions that the Court may 
impose on him for its return.  
2.4. By order dated 22.02.2015, Additional Sessions 
Judge rejected his application. The Court 

--- Page 165 ---
WP(Crl.)No.422 of 2026  3 
 
declined to release the revolver in view of the 
pending appeal against the order of acquittal.  
2.5. Aggrieved, the petitioner filed Criminal 
Application No. 4811 of 2014 under section 482 
CrPC before the High Court praying for setting 
aside of order rejecting his application under 
section 452 CrPC and release of the revolver.  
2.6. By order dated 09.03.2015, the High Court 
directed that the petitioner’s application be kept 
along with the appeals against the judgment of 
acquittal. The said application and also the 
appeals have remained pending since 2014.  
2.7.  Aggrieved, the petitioner is here before us. 
3. Heard learned counsel for the parties.  
4. The principal grievance of the petitioner is that his 
licensed revolver continues to remain in the custody of 
the authorities despite his acquittal in the criminal 
trial. In addition to that, his application seeking its 
release has remained pending before the High Court for 
several years.  
5. The High Court deferred the consideration of 
petitioner’s application under section 482 CrPC and 
directed that the same be kept along with the appeals 
pending against the judgment of acquittal. It is 
important to note that the pendency of appeals by itself 

--- Page 166 ---
WP(Crl.)No.422 of 2026  4 
 
does not determine petitioner’s entitlement for the 
return of the revolver. Both the Courts below have failed 
to consider the application on its own merits, and 
instead allowed the pendency of appeals to impede its 
adjudication. 
6. At this stage, it is imperative to take into consideration 
the prolonged time period for which the petitioner has 
been deprived of his licensed revolver. The revolver was 
seized in 2012 and the petitioner was acquitted by the 
Sessions Court on 11.09.2013. Despite the passage of 
more than a decade since his acquittal, the revolver 
continues to remain in the custody of the authorities.  
7. Section 452 CrPC empowers the criminal court to pass 
appropriate orders regarding disposal of property at the 
conclusion of an inquiry or trial. The exercise of this 
power requires the court to ascertain whether the 
property ought to be returned or retaine d, having 
regard to the facts and circumstances of the case. The 
underlying principle of the provision, as recognized by 
this Court in several decisions, is that any seized 
property ought not to remain in the custody of the 
police or the court for any time  longer than what is 
absolutely necessary. In the present case, the petitioner 
has been acquitted of all charges levelled against him, 
and no material has been brought to our notice 

--- Page 167 ---
WP(Crl.)No.422 of 2026  5 
 
indicating any other ground which may necessitate the 
continued retention of the revolver. In these 
circumstances, the mere pendency of appeals against 
acquittal cannot by itself justify withholding the return 
of the revolver, without examining the petitioner’s claim 
on its merits.  
8. The prolonged retention of the revolver has also had 
consequences for petitioner’s livelihood. He is employed 
in the private security sector and possession of the 
revolver is necessary for him to secure employment in 
that field. The record also reflects that he is responsible 
for maintaining a family of six members. Having been 
deprived of his revolver since 2012, the petitioner has 
been left to contend with the consequences of its 
continued retention for over a decade. The application 
for its return has re mained undecided on merits 
throughout this period.  
9. In view of the foregoing, we are of the considered view 
that the continued retention of the revolver is not 
warranted in the facts and circumstances of the 
present case. Mere pendency of appeal against 
acquittal, cannot by itself, justify its continued 
retention.  
10. Accordingly, the writ petition is allowed. The 
respondent-State is directed to take necessary steps to 

--- Page 168 ---
WP(Crl.)No.422 of 2026  6 
 
ensure that the custody of the revolver bearing License 
No.9040, NPB No. 4571 is handed over to the 
petitioner, subject to compliance with the applicable 
requirements under the Arms Act, 1959. The same 
shall be done within eight weeks from the date of 
receipt of this order.  
11. In view of the directions issued hereinabove, Criminal 
Application No. 4811 of 2014 pending before the High 
Court of Judicature of Bombay at Aurangabad shall 
stand disposed of. Needless to say, this order shall not 
affect the proceedings in the pending appeal before the 
High Court.  
12. Pending applications, if any, shall stand disposed of.

[VIKRAM NATH] 
 
 
……………………………..J. 
[R. MAHADEVAN] 
 
 
……………………………..J.

                       RECORD OF PROCEEDINGS

[Arising out of impugned final judgment and order dated 24-07-2026

1. Leave granted.

3. This  appeal  arises  from  an  order  dated
07.09.2026  passed  by  the  High  Court  of
Judicature at Madras rejecting the regular
bail prayer of the appellant in connection
with Crime No.139 of 2026 registered with
Sathuvachari P.S., Tamil Nadu.
4. As per the prosecution case, a parcel booked
in the name of one Yuvraj Singh was received
by the college administration. When the said
Crl.A. @ SLP (Crl.) No.17589/2026                                                     1

--- Page 176 ---
parcel was opened, ten strips of 100 tablets
of Tapentadol Hydrocholoride of 100 mg were
found. Based on material collected during
investigation, the appellant was implicated.
5. The submission of the learned counsel for the
appellant is that his complicity is based on
confessional  statement  of  the  co-accused.
Besides, there is no basis to implicate the
appellant  for  offences  punishable  under
Sections 111 and 123 of the Bhartiya Nyaya
Sanhita, 2023.
6. Additionally, it is submitted that even if
those tablets were to be consumed or used by
the appellant, since those drugs do not fall
in the category of Narcotic and Psychotropic
Substances, there would be no serious offence
made out.  Moreover, an offence punishable
under Section 111 of BNS is not made out as
there is no unlawful activity contemplated
therein;  besides,  no  more  than  one
chargesheet in any such specified crime has
been filed. 
7. It has been also submitted that although in
the counter affidavit it is stated that there
is  one  more  case  registered  against  the

--- Page 177 ---
appellant, but it has not come on record that
after investigation any charge-sheet has been
submitted  in  that  case.  In  such
circumstances, it is submitted, the appellant
being a student is entitled to be released on
bail. More so when there is no allegation
that he has served or administered any drug
to any person.
8. The learned counsel for the respondent-State
has opposed the prayer for bail but could not
dispute that complicity of the appellant is
based  on  confessional  statement  of  co-
accused, and that there is no recovery of any
incriminating article including drug from the
appellant.
9. Having  regard  to  the  above,  without
expressing  any  opinion  on  merits  of  the
prosecution case, we are of the view that the
appellant is entitled to be released on bail
in this case, pending trial.

order passed by the High Court rejecting the
bail prayer of the appellant is set aside.

UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. The issue is in a very narrow compass as to the
participation of the petitioner in the proceedings before
the  Lucknow  Development  Authority  (for  short,  ‘the
Authority’) which has been initiated under Section 27 of
the U.P. Urban Planning and Development Act, 1973 (the Act
of 1973) which notice has been issued against the 5th
respondent  herein.  The  5th  respondent  challenged  the
proceedings before the High Court, in which an order was
passed, directing the writ petitioner to file a detailed
response to the notice with all relevant documents and any
report in their favour, upon which the Authority was given
2

--- Page 189 ---
          SLP(C) NO.37043 OF 2026
liberty to carry out inspection by an officer of the rank
not less than that of Chief Engineer/Additional Secretary
within four weeks thereafter. The High Court also directed
consideration of the same independently and impartially
without being influenced by any further action at the
behest of the CMS, the petitioner herein.
2. Mr. Kapil Sibal, learned Senior Counsel appeared for
the petitioner submitted that the petitioner cannot be
kept away from the hearing and the petitioner does not
have any objection with respect to the other portion of
the  judgment,  including  that  of  an  inspection  and
consideration to be made independently and impartially.
3. Ms. Malvik Trivedi, learned Senior Counsel appearing
for the respondent, however, submitted that there is a
history of the dispute between the two parties and the
petitioner has been constantly trying to take over the
property in the possession of the 5th respondent.  It is
also submitted that as of now, an order dated 21.10.2026
has been passed by the Authority in Suit No.2092 of 2025,
Online Case No.LDA/Z6/ANI/2025/0006284.
3

--- Page 190 ---
          SLP(C) NO.37043 OF 2026
4. On brief facts, it is to be noticed that a total area
of 23000 sq. ft. was owned by Smt. Urmila Bhalla and
Smt. Sheela Kapoor. Out of the total extent 6000 sq. ft.
was leased out by the 5th respondent’s predecessor, and
17000 sq. ft. was leased out by City Montessori School,
the petitioner herein. There were multiple proceedings
initiated  for  eviction  of  the  CMS  which  eventually
culminated in an acquisition being carried out for the
purposes of the CMS. However, when such acquisition was
proceeded with, the entire 23000 sq. ft. was acquired
which was successfully challenged in a Writ Petition.  The
challenge to this Court resulted in the acquisition being
upheld for 17000 sq. ft. relating to CMS, while setting it
aside insofar 6000 sq. ft.  While the matter was pending
before this Court, the 6000 sq. ft. was also conceded to
the lessee by the Government. The present proceedings were
initiated at the behest of the CMS, alleging unauthorized
constructions.  The  dispute  with  respect  to  the
unauthorized construction also went through various rounds
and eventually it has ended with the present notice under
4

--- Page 191 ---
          SLP(C) NO.37043 OF 2026
Section 27 issued under the Act of 1973.
5. We need not touch upon the merits of the dispute or
the allegation of unauthorized construction. Suffice it to
notice that the direction was only to consider the issue
independently and impartially, without being influenced by
any action carried out at the behest of CMS. This is not
to say that the CMS should not be heard, especially when
it is on their initiative, the complaint was filed.
Whether the allegation is valid or not is definitely left
to the independent and impartial consideration of the
Authority. But it could never have been intended that the
complainant is kept away from the proceedings. The order
passed on 21.10.2026 obviously is not after affording a
hearing to the CMS.
6. In such circumstances, we set aside the order dated
21.10.2026 only to facilitate fresh consideration.  The
Authority shall issue notice both to the CMS and the 5th
respondent and shall supply a copy of the reply and the
Annexures produced by the 5th respondent to the CMS.  If
any inspection report is on record, as indicated by the
5

--- Page 192 ---
          SLP(C) NO.37043 OF 2026
impugned judgment, then the same also shall be served on
the parties.  The notice shall indicate a date within one
month from today and on the said date or any other date to
which  the  hearing  is  adjourned,  with  acknowledgment
personally taken from the parties or their authorized
representatives who appear on the first day, the matter
shall be concluded. We make it clear that we have not
looked into the merits of the order passed by the High
Court on 21.10.2026 and have interfered with it only on
the grounds of violation of the principles of natural
justice. The matter shall be considered on its own merits,
in accordance with law.
7. The Special Leave Petition stands disposed of with
the above directions.
8. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand rejected.
(CHANDRESH)                        (POOJA SHARMA)

O R D E R
1. During the pendency of this case, the parties were referred to
the Supreme Court Mediation Centre to explore the possibility
of an amicable settlement of their disputes. Pursuant to the
efforts made by the learned Mediator, the parties settled their
differences and reduced the terms of their compromise to
writing, vide Settlement Agreement dated 12.12.2025.  Pursuant
thereto, they have now filed joint applications in I.A. Nos.
169425/2026 and 119511/2026, seeking appropriate directions
from this Court.
2. The parties got married on 10.12.2017 but they have been living
separately since May, 2022. Their daughter is still a minor. 
3. In terms of the Settlement Agreement, the respondent-husband
agreed to pay a sum of 35,00,000/- (Rupees thirty five lakhs₹
only) to the petitioner-wife in full and final settlement of
all  her  claims.  We  are  informed  by  the  learned  counsel
appearing for the parties that the total amount as on date has
1

--- Page 194 ---
been paid to the petitioner-wife. Mr. Siddharth Anil Khanna,
learned counsel, appearing for the petitioner-wife, confirms
that she has received the full amount.
4. We may note that, though the parties included a clause in the
Settlement Agreement that the payment made by the respondent-
husband would settle all the daughter’s claims also, we are not
willing to accept the same. The rights of the daughter as
against her f ather, be it in relation to her share in his
ancestral property or for her own maintenance and education,
shall not be affected by the Settlement Agreement between her
parents.  Though it would be open to the mother to use part of
the settlement amount for the betterment of her daughter’s
future, however, the same shall not preclude the daughter from
asserting her rights against her father at an appropriate
stage. 
5. The parties having been living apart since May, 2022, and in
the light of the settlement of the disputes by and between
them, we find no reason to prolong their marital relationship
or  keep  the  litigation  initiated  by  them  pending.  We,
accordingly, exercise our jurisdiction under Article 142 of the
Constitution of India, and dissolve the marriage performed by
and between them on 10.12.2017.

CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.           OF 2026
(@ SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (CRIMINAL) NO.18661/2026)
NAROTAM BEHERA & ORS.      APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
STATE OF CHHATTISGARH       RESPONDENT(S)
ORDER
1. Leave granted.
2. We have heard Mr. Ratnakar Dash, learned Senior
counsel for the appellants and Mr. Aman, learned counsel
for the respondent-State of Chhattisgarh.
3. There are 03 appellants in this appeal. They are
Narotam Behera, Shiv Sahu and Shushil Kumar Sahu.
4. Appellants are aggrieved by order dated 12.05.2026
passed by the High Court of Chhattisgarh at Bilaspur
(briefly the ‘High Court’ hereinafter), rejecting their
regular bail application.
5. Appellants are accused in Crime No.20/2026 registered
at  Police  Station-  Singhoda,  District-  Mahasamund,
Chhattisgarh, under Sections 20(b)(ii)(C) and 29(1) of the
Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985 (for
short, ‘NDPS Act’).
1

--- Page 204 ---
6. Appellants were arrested on 24.02.2026 and has been
in custody since then.
7. This  Court  had  issued  notice  vide  order  dated
21.09.2026,  pursuant  to  which  respondent-State  of
Chhattisgarh has filed counter affidavit.
8. In the case of co-accused Budhu Bhutiya, this Court,
vide  order  dated  16.09.2026,  had  granted  him  bail.
Relevant portion of the order dated 16.09.2026 is as
under:
“8. We have duly considered the submissions
made and have also perused the materials on
record. We find that in all there are eight
accused persons. Total quantity of contraband
seized is 137 kilograms. As of now, there is no
apportionment of the contraband between the
accused persons. This is relevant because the
commercial  quantity  of  ganja  is  twenty
kilograms or more. We further find that the co-
accused have already been enlarged on bail by
the Court. Investigation is complete whereafter
charge-sheet has been filed though the charges
have not yet been framed.
9. In such circumstances, we are inclined to
grant bail to the appellant. Consequently, we
set aside the impugned order of the High Court
dated 14.05.2026 and direct that the appellant
shall be produced before the jurisdictional
Special Court within a maximum period of seven
days from today whereafter he shall be enlarged
on bail on such terms and conditions as may be
deemed appropriate.”
9. On due consideration, we are of the opinion that the
2

--- Page 205 ---
same benefit may be extended to the appellants as well.
10. That being the position, t he impugned order dated
12.05.2026 passed by the High Court is set aside.
11. Consequently, we direct that the appellants shall be
produced before the jurisdictional Special Court within a
maximum period of 07 days from today, whereafter they
shall be released on bail on such terms and conditions as
may be deemed appropriate. We further direct that the
appellant(s) shall appear on each and every date of
hearing before the Trial Court except on such occasions
when his presence may be exempted by the Trial Court.
12. Accordingly, the Criminal Appeal is allowed.
13. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
MISCELLANEOUS APPLICATION No(s). 2839-2840 OF 2026
IN
[SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (CRIMINAL) No(s). 3197-3198 OF 2024]
SATISH NATHALAL GOGHARI    APPLICANT(S)/
     PETITIONER(S)
VERSUS
THE STATE OF MAHARASHTRA       NON-APPLICANT(S)/
     RESPONDENT(S)
ORDER
1. We have heard learned counsel for the applicant as
well  as  learned  counsel  for  the  respondent-State  of
Maharashtra.
2. These Miscellaneous Application(s) have been filed by
the applicant for modification of the condition imposed by
this Court while granting bail to the applicant vide order
dated 03.05.2024 in Special Leave Petition (Criminal)
No(s).3197-3198/2024.
3. Applicant  is  an  accused  in  FIR  No.67  of  2019
registered  at  Police  Station-  Kanjurmarg,  District-
1

--- Page 209 ---
Mumbai, Maharashtra under Sections 406 and 420 of the
Indian Penal Code, 1860 (for short, ‘IPC’) read with
Sections 3 and 4 of the Maharashtra Ownership Flats
(Regulation  of  the  Promotion  of  Construction,  Sale,
Management and Transfer) Act, 1963.
4. After the bail prayer of the applicant was rejected
by the High Court of Judicature at Bombay (briefly ‘the
High Court’ hereinafter), applicant had preferred Special
Leave Petition (Criminal) No(s).3197-3198/2024 before this
Court.
5. Vide the order dated 03.05.2024, this Court noted
that while the petitioner was in custody since 23.09.2019,
no  progress  was  made  in  the  trial.  Notwithstanding
submission of charge-sheet, charges were not framed at
that point of time.
6. We find from the order dated 03.05.2024 that learned
counsel for the applicant made a statement before the
Court that he would deposit an amount of Rs.50,00,000/-
within 04 weeks from the date of his release.
7. This  Court,  taking  the  view  that  continued
incarceration of the applicant violated Article 21 of the
Constitution of India, directed release of the applicant
on bail with further direction to the Trial Court to
conclude  the  trial  expeditiously.  In  view  of  the
undertaking given by learned counsel for the applicant,
this Court directed that applicant should deposit an
amount of Rs.50,00,000/- within 04 weeks from the date of
2

--- Page 210 ---
release and a further amount of Rs.50,00,000/- within a
period of 08 weeks thereafter.
8. In the Miscellaneous Application(s), it is stated by
the applicant that despite his best efforts, he could not
comply with the condition imposed by this Court regarding
deposit  of  Rs.1,00,00,000/-,  in  two  tranches  of
Rs.50,00,000/- each, because of extreme financial hardship
due to collapse of his business. He has further stated
that he has already undergone more than 05 years of
incarceration.
9. In the hearing today, Ms.  Rukhmini Bobde, learned
counsel for the respondent-State of Maharashtra submits
that as of today, cross-examination of P.W.3 is going on.
10. On a query by the Court, she submits that as many as
75 prosecution witnesses remain to be examined.
11. Having  regard  to  the  totality  of  the  facts  and
circumstances of the case, we are of the view that
notwithstanding the undertaking given by learned counsel
for  the  applicant,  insistence  on  deposit  of
Rs.1,00,00,000/-, in two tranches of Rs.50,00,000/- each,
would be oppressive. It has turned out to be an onerous
condition  facilitating  continued  incarceration  of  the
applicant for about 2 ½ years even after this Court had
directed his release on the ground of violation of Article
21 of the Constitution of India.
12. Accordingly, we recall the following portion of the
order dated 03.05.2024 passed in Special Leave Petition
3

--- Page 211 ---
(Criminal) No(s).3197-3198/2024:
“However, it shall be on his undertaking that
he would deposit and amount of Rs.50,00,000/-
(Rupees Fifty Lakhs only) within four weeks
from the date of release and a further amount
of Rs.50,00,000/- (Rupees Fifty Lakhs only)
within a further period of eight weeks.”
13. Consequently,  the  applicant  shall  be  forthwith
released on bail on usual terms and conditions. However,
the applicant shall co-operate with the ongoing trial.
14. Accordingly,  the  Miscellaneous  Application(s)  are
allowed.
15. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.

INHERENT JURISDICTION
 CONTEMPT PETITION (C) NO. 160/2026
IN
CIVIL APPEAL NO. 5686/2023
RAM KRISHNA RAM                                    Petitioner
                                VERSUS
SHRI RAJESH P. RUIA, SECRETARY & ORS.              Respondents
O R D E R
1. The  contempt  proceedings  have  been  initiated  for  alleged  wilful
disobedience of the order dated 05.09.2023, passed by this Court, particularly
the  direction  issued  in  paragraph  No.7  of  the  said  order.  For  immediate
reference, the direction issued in the aforesaid order is extracted hereinbelow:-
“7. Having  regard  to  the  totality  of  the  circumstances,  the
respondents are hereby directed to calculate the appellant's back
wages @ 40% till date of appellant's superannuation and also
ensure that all terminal benefits are calculated on the basis of his
notional  continuity  in  service,  including  gratuity,  notional
increments and fixing the last salary drawn, for pension purposes
based  on  such  increase  (notionally)  of  salary  and  all
consequential  benefits.  These  amounts  shall  be  worked-out
through appropriate calculations within eight weeks from today.
The appellant's pension shall be fixed within that time-frame. All
the amounts in aggregate shall be paid to the appellant within
twelve weeks. It is open to the respondents — school to recover
the amount from the State Government in case of any shortfall.
The State Government is directed to do whatever is necessary to
be done in this regard.”
1

--- Page 219 ---
2. At the outset it requires to be noticed that State was never made a party
in the Civil Appeal No.5686/2023 (Arising out of SLP (C) No. 10571/2021). As
such  there  is  an  initial  flaw  in  directing  the  contemnor(s)/respondent(s)  to
recover the amount from the State Government in case of any shortfall. On
account of the name of the State Government having surfaced in the order
dated 05.09.2023 the complainant has arrayed the Chief Secretary and the
Principal Secretary as the contemnor/respondent nos. 2 and 3 respectively in
the present contempt proceedings. There being no direction or order to the
State Government to pay the amount to the complainant, the continuation of
the present contempt proceedings against the contemnor/respondent nos. 2
and 3 is not warranted and accordingly, the contempt proceedings against them
are dropped.
3. Coming to the core issue, namely, as to whether the direction issued by
this Court  vide  order dated 05.09.2023 has been complied with or there has
been wilful disobedience, it would not retain us for too long to close the present
contempt proceedings for reasons more than one. Firstly, the direction that has
been  issued  in  the  aforesaid  order  as  extracted  hereinabove  is  clear  and
explicit,  namely  back  wages  @  of  40%  till  the  date  of  appellant’s
superannuation  is  to  be  calculated  and  paid  and  the
respondent(s)/contemnor(s)  have  also  been  directed  that  they  should  also
ensure that all terminal benefits are calculated on the basis of his notional
continuity in service, including gratuity, notional increments and by fixing the
last salary drawn, for pension purposes based on such increase (notionally) of
salary and all consequential benefits the amounts are to be paid.  Secondly, in
the reply affidavit filed, it has been clearly stated at Annexure R-3 the summary
2

--- Page 220 ---
of the salary to which the complainant would be entitled to for the period from
1974 to 2005 (date of superannuation) which would be Rs.17,23,377/- has been
paid and thirdly, the DCRG amount has also been calculated and as ordered by
this Court has been paid @ 40%. Thus, it cannot be gainsaid by the complainant
that there has been any disobedience, much less wilful disobedience, of the
order passed by this Court.
4. In view of the same, the order of this Court having been complied with as
understood  by  the  contemnor(s)/respondent(s),  continuation  of  the  present
contempt  proceedings  would  not  be  warranted  and  accordingly,  the  same
stands closed. However, we make it clear that in the event of there being any
claim  arising  out  of  the  calculation  reflected  in  Annexure  R-3  of  the  reply
affidavit, the complainant/petitioner would be at liberty to challenge the same
in an independent proceedings and all contentions in that regard are kept open.
5. Accordingly, the contempt proceedings stand closed.
6. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NO.               OF 2026
(@SLP (C) No.27954 of 2026)
M/S RADHIKA PROJECTS PRIVATE LIMITED ..... APPELLANT(S)

M/S J B HOMES BUILDERS AND DEVELOPERS ..... RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. Heard.
2. Leave granted.
3. Appellant herein was the petitioner before the High Court and he was the
unsuccessful respondent in an arbitral proceeding, namely, having suffered
an award, challenged the same by filing a petition under Section 34 of the
Arbitration  and  Conciliation  Act,  1996  before  the  Commercial  Court.  The
Commercial Court had agreed to stay the award conditionally and directed
the appellant herein to deposit a sum of Rs.1,02,50,000/- (Rupees One Crore
Two Lakhs Fifty Thousand) within 10 days and the same was not deposited
and as such the application for stay stood closed.
1

--- Page 229 ---
4. Challenging the said order before the High Court and seeking extension
revision was filed. The High Court extended the timeline on 23.07.2026 and
further  opportunity  was  granted  on  27.07.2026.  A  prayer  was  made  on
30.07.2026 seeking for further extension by two months. However, the High
Court by order  dated 04.08.2026  recorded the statement of the counsel
which was to the effect that payment would be made by 07.08.2026 and
granted  time  accordingly.  However,  even  said  agreed  timeline  was  not
complied with.
5. The  order  dated 04.08.2026  passed by  the  high  Court,  is  challenged
before this Court. While issuing notice on 14.08.2026, this court recorded the
submissions made by the learned senior counsel appearing for the appellant
and passed the following order:
“1. The learned senior counsel appearing for the petitioner would
submit that amount of Rs. 1,02,50,000/- (Rs. One Crore Two Lakh
Fifty Thousand only) which was agreed to be paid on or before
07.08.2026, for multifarious reasons could not be arranged and as
such to exhibit the  bona fides  of the petitioner, they are ready
and willing to deposit today itself a sum of Rs. 25,00,000/- (Rs.
Twenty Five lakh only) and balance amount within such time as
may be ordered. In view of same amount i.e., Rs. 25,00,000/- (Rs.
Twenty Five  lakh only)  shall be deposited by 18.08.2026.  The
balance  amount  shall  be  deposited  on  or  before  25.08.2026.
Hence, issue notice, returnable in four weeks.
2. The execution proceedings shall remain stayed till the next
date of hearing.”
6. Mr. Sanjay Nuli, learned senior counsel appearing for respondent(s) would
fairly submits that amount has since been deposited. Thus, petition(s) under
Section 34 of the  Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 stand(s) is revived
and we request the jurisdictional Commercial Court adjudicating petition(s)
2

--- Page 230 ---
filed under Section 34, namely, C.O.P. No.57 of 2026, to be disposed of
expeditiously preferably within a period of three months from today, subject
to both the parties cooperating with the Court.
7. It is needless to state that parties would be at liberty to resolve the
dispute amicably, if they deem fit.
8. The appeal stands disposed of accordingly.
9. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NO.      /2026
@ SLP (C) NO.33889/2025
ASHOK KUMAR         APPELLANT
                            VERSUS
KEWAL KRISHAN & ORS.        RESPONDENTS
O R D E R
1. Heard.
2. Leave granted.
3. The order dated 10.11.2025 is under challenge before this Court
whereunder  the  jurisdictional  High  Court  has  allowed  the
Revision Petition filed by respondent No.1 herein and directed
the jurisdictional Court to draw the final decree-sheet pursuant
to the final decree dated 04.03.2024  within  a period  of  two
months from the date of the order.
4. Having heard the learned counsels appearing for the parties and
on  perusal  of  the  entire  records,  it  would  clearly  emerge
therefrom  that subsequent to the passing of the preliminary
decree on 24.08.2017, the final decree came to be passed on
1

--- Page 244 ---
04.03.2024. However, it is the case of the appellant herein that
pursuant to the said final decree, there was discussion between
the  parties  which  resulted  in  a  settlement  agreement  being
entered into on 25.07.2024 between parties and as such an
application  under  Order  XXIII  Rule  3  of  the  Code  of  Civil
Procedure, 1908 (for short, “CPC”) was filed in C.S. No.243/2021
before the jurisdictional Court with a prayer to dispose of the
matter  in  terms  of  the  Memorandum  recording  family
settlement dated 25.07.2024. However, after a period of one
year,  objections  came  to  be  filed  to  the  said  application  by
respondent  No.1  herein,  i.e.,  on  20.08.2025  and  these  facts
being well within the knowledge of respondent(s) herein, yet
suppressing these facts and depicting as though there are no
proceedings  pending  before  trial  court  and  for  the  alleged
enforcement of the final decree dated 04.03.2024, Civil Revision
Petition under Article 227 of the Constitution of India came to be
filed seeking for a direction to the jurisdictional Court to draw
the  final  decree  in  C.S.  No.365/2017  dated  04.03.2024.
Surprisingly,  the  High  Court  has  also  not  issued  notice  to
respondent No.1, namely, the appellant herein. In fact, the copy
of the Civil Revision Petition is not placed on record. The fact
that application filed under Order XXIII Rule 3 of the CPC (by the
appellant and respondent Nos.2 to 5 herein at Annexure P5) and
the objections filed on 20.08.2025 (by respondent No.1 herein)
2

--- Page 245 ---
seems to have not been brought to the notice of the High Court.
Obviously,  the  fact  of  the  final  decree  having  not  been
crystallized seems to have swayed in the mind of the High Court
to issue a direction to conclude the said proceedings. In the
event of either of the parties had brought it to the notice of the
High Court about the pendency of the application filed under
Order XXIII  Rule 3  of the CPC or objection filed thereto which
was pending consideration, the impugned order would not have
been passed. The appellant herein was not even issued with the
notice in the Revision Petition, and as such the appellant could
not bring these facts to the notice of the High Court also. No
blame can be laid at the doors of the appellant herein. In fact,
respondent No.1 herein, who had approached the jurisdictional
High Court under Article 227 of the Constitution of India, ought
to have disclosed all the material facts before the High Court
including the factum of an application under Order XXIII Rule 3
of  the  CPC  and  objection  to same  having been filed by the
parties. In the light of the said fact having not been brought to
the notice of the High Court, the impugned order came to be
passed and as such impugned order cannot be sustained for two
reasons:
(i) Firstly, on account of notice having not been issued to
the appellant herein;
3

--- Page 246 ---
(ii) Secondly,  on  account  of  respondent  No.1  herein
having not disclosed before the High Court about the
pendency of the application filed under Order XXIII
Rule 1 of the CPC by appellant and objection filed to
said application by 1st Respondent herein.
Hence,  the  impugned  order  is  set  aside.  The  Revision
Petition stands restored to the file of the High Court for being
disposed  of  in  accordance  with  law  by  taking  note  of  the
application  filed  under  Order  XXIII  Rule  3  of  the  CPC  and
objections filed thereto. Accordingly, appeal is allowed.
5. No order as to costs. All pending application stand consigned to
records.

(VIPUL M. PANCHOLI)

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
INHERENT JURISDICTION
Curative Petition (Civil) No. 446 / 2026
Manjula and others   …Appellant(s)
versus
D.A. Srinivas         …Respondent(s)
in Review Petition (Civil) No. 10500 / 2026
in Civil Appeal No. 7370 / 2026
ORDER
1. Application seeking listing of the Curative Petition in open Court is rejected.
2. The instant Petition seeks partial recall/modification of the detailed judgment
dated 08.05.2026 passed in Civil Appeal No. 7370/2026, whereby a two-
Judge Bench of this Court, comprising two of us (J.B. Pardiwala and R.
Mahadevan, JJ.),  disposed of  the appeal filed by the Curative Petitioners.
They,  however,  are  aggrieved  by  certain  findings  recorded  and  the
consequential directions issued in the said judgment.
3. We have gone through the Curative Petitions and the relevant documents
placed before us.
4. Upon considering the matter in its entirety, the two-Judge Bench noted that,
in  the  application  filed  under  Order  VII  Rule  11  of  the  Code  of  Civil
Procedure, 1908 (CPC) seeking rejection of the plaint, the Curative Petitioners
Page 1 of 5

--- Page 254 ---
had  categorically  asserted  that  the  properties  claimed  by  Respondent
(Plaintiff in the Civil Suit) were the subject matter of a benami transaction.
Ultimately,  the  two-Judge  Bench  disposed  of  the  Civil  Appeal  with  a
consequential direction for taking over the suit properties in accordance with
law, having regard to the fact that the judicial determination declaring the
transaction to be benami had attained finality.
5. Section  5  of  the  Prohibition  of  Benami  Property  Transactions  Act,  1988
provides for the confiscation of property held to be  benami, subject to the
provisions  of  the  said  legislation.  Confiscation,  therefore,  follows  upon  a
determination in accordance with law that the property is benami.
6. In the instant case, the Curative Petitioners themselves asserted, in their
application under Order VII Rule 11 of the CPC, that the properties were the
subject matter of a benami transaction. The Respondent (Plaintiff in the Civil
Suit) has not disputed this Court’s acceptance of the said assertion. In such
circumstances, the Curative Petitioners have failed to make out any ground
warranting  interference  with  the  findings  recorded  or  the  consequential
directions issued by the two-Judge Bench.
7. In view of the foregoing and having regard to the parameters indicated in
Rupa  Ashok  Hurra  vs.  Ashok  Hurra  &  Anr.,1 we  find  no  reason  to
entertain this Petition or to exercise our inherent curative jurisdiction.
1  (2002) 4 SCC 388.
Page 2 of 5

--- Page 255 ---
8. The Curative Petition is, accordingly, dismissed.
9. As a result, the pending application(s), if any, also stand disposed of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA

CRIMINAL APPEAL No.        OF 2026
[ARISING OUT OF SLP (CRIMINAL) NO.  12326/2026  ]
DHARMENDRA KOONT                             APPELLANT(S)
                                VERSUS
 STATE OF RAJASTHAN                           RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
    1.   Leave granted.
2.  The present appeal has been filed by the appellant
seeking bail in connection with FIR No.509/2023 dated
06.11.2023  registered  at  Police  Station  Amer,  Jaipur,
Rajasthan for offences punishable under Sections 304-B and
120-B of the Indian Penal Code, 1860. The appellant is in
jail for the last 2 years 11 months.
3. Learned counsel for the appellant has stated before
this Court that earlier the appellant went along with his
wife to lodge a First Information Report against his own
parents as they were harassing his wife. The wife has later
on committed suicide. There is certainly a suicide note
on record.
4. Learned counsel for the appellant submits that the
trial is not progressing and the appellant is in jail for
almost 3 years and therefore keeping in view the period of
CRIMINAL APPEAL No.        OF 2026
[ARISING OUT OF SLP (CRIMINAL) NO.  12326/2026  ]

--- Page 279 ---
2
incarceration, the application for grant of bail may be
allowed.  On  the  other  hand,  learned  counsel  for  the
respondent-State has vehemently opposed the prayer for
grant of bail. She has stated that there is enough material
against the appellant and the bail petition be rejected
accordingly.
5. Having regard to the nature of allegations and the
period of incarceration of the appellant, we find that his
further detention in custody is unnecessary; hence, we are
inclined to accept the appeal and grant relief as prayed by
admitting the appellant to an order for grant of bail.
6. Accordingly, we set aside the impugned order passed
by the High Court.
7. Appellant shall be released on bail, subject to
furnishing of bail bonds to the satisfaction of the trial
court and subject to such other terms and conditions as may
be imposed by it.
8. Needless  to  observe,  the  appellant  shall  not,
directly or indirectly, by making inducement, threat or
promise, dissuade any person acquainted with the facts of
the case from disclosing such facts to the court.
9.  In the event there is any breach of the terms and
conditions for grant of bail, the trial court shall be at
liberty to cancel the bail of the appellant.
CRIMINAL APPEAL No.        OF 2026
[ARISING OUT OF SLP (CRIMINAL) NO.  12326/2026  ]

--- Page 280 ---
3
10.  It  is  also  ordered  that  the  appellant  shall
diligently attend proceedings of the trial unless exempted,
If he is found to abstain from attending the proceedings
without justifiable cause, that could also be seen as
breach of the conditions for grant of bail and the trial
court shall be free to pass appropriate orders.
11. We clarify that the observations made in this order
and grant of bail will not be treated as findings on the
merits of the case.
12. The appeal is, accordingly, allowed on the aforesaid
terms.

5
CRIMINAL APPEAL No.        OF 2026
[ARISING OUT OF SLP (CRIMINAL) NO.  12326/2026  ]

--- Page 283 ---
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL  NO.         OF 2026
(arising out of SLP (C) No.  23859/2025)
JANARDHAN DASS            ...APPELLANT(S) 
                                VERSUS
KIRNESH JUNG                   ...RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. The present appeal has been filed challenging the
impugned judgment dated 10.04.2025 passed by the High
Court of Himachal Pradesh at Shimla in C.M.P.(M) No.
312/2023, wherein, the application seeking condonation
of delay in filing the second appeal by the appellant
has been dismissed.
3. The appellant is the plaintiff in Civil Suit No.
21/1 of 2011/13/15. The prayer in the suit was to cancel
the  sale  deed  dated  26.05.2010,  executed  between
plaintiff  and  the  defendant-respondent  for  the  suit
properties,  subsequent  mutation  entries  and  for
injunction to  restrain the defendant from entering into
1

--- Page 284 ---
the suit properties.
4. The Trial Court was pleased to partly decree the
suit to the extent of cancelling the sale deed dated
26.05.2010, subject to the repayment of Rs. 6,40,000/-
to the respondent by the appellant out of the total
consideration of Rs. 16,50,000/-, and also granted the
relief of injunction. The First Appellate Court, allowed
the  appeal  filed  by  the  defendant-respondent  and
dismissed the suit. Aggrieved, the appellant preferred
an application seeking condonation of delay in filing
the regular second appeal. 
5. We have heard the learned counsel appearing for the
appellant and learned Senior counsel appearing for the
respondent.
6. Learned counsel appearing for the appellant would
submit that the judgment of the First Appellate Court
though a reasoned one, was passed  ex parte.  In such
view, there was a delay in filing the second appeal
coupled with the COVID-19 pandemic in the interregnum.
However, the said factors have not been taken into
consideration by the High Court.
7. Learned Senior counsel appearing for the respondent
would submit that the delay is beyond the set-off period
of COVID-19 and, in any case, the judgment cannot be
termed as having been rendered ex parte.
2

--- Page 285 ---
8. We are dealing with a case where the Trial Court has
partly decreed the suit in favour of the appellant,
while the Appellate Court set aside the decree, without
hearing the appellant. The second appeal was dismissed
by the High Court refusing to condone the delay in
filing the same.
9. On perusal of the judgment passed by the First
Appellate Court, we find that the decree in favour of
the appellant has been set aside ex parte.  Considering
the facts, we are inclined to hold that the appellant is
certainly  entitled  to  the  relief  of  condonation  of
delay, as merely the duration of delay per se, cannot be
a  ground  to  reject  the  substantive  right  of  the
appellant, especially, when it involves reversing the
decision of the Trial Court. The Courts are not expected
to adopt such a pedantic approach, while adjudicating an
application under Section 5 of the Limitation Act, 1963.
10. Taking note of the aforesaid facts, we are inclined
to set aside the impugned order whereby the condonation
of delay application filed by the appellant has been
rejected. However, we make it clear that we have not
expressed anything on the merits of the case.
11. Liberty is granted to the appellant to file an
appropriate  application  for  impleading  the  proposed
party, as during the pendency of the proceedings, the
3

--- Page 286 ---
respondent is stated to have alienated the property in
favour of the said proposed party.
12. The appeal is, accordingly, allowed.
13. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.

                                      (M.M. SUNDRESH )
 
…………………………………………………………J.

1. This is a matter pertaining to custody dispute.

1

--- Page 289 ---
2. The petitioner/mother succeeded before the Trial
Court but the High Court has, on the ground that the
Trial  Court  has  not  examined  the  issue  of
maintainability, remitted the matter back to the Trial
Court.  The net result is today the petitioner has not
been able to meet two girls aged approximately 17 years
and 13 years.  Whatever be the legal issues that may be
involved, there cannot be a situation where a mother is
not allowed to meet her two daughters, who are minors.
There are rival versions as to why the mother is not able
to meet the children but we are, for the present, not
adverting to the same.  We are of the opinion that as and
when the mother desires and, of course, subject to mutual
convenience, the mother and the girls should interact.
Any differences also ought to be sorted out.

petitioner/mother  and  the  daughters,  we  direct  as
follows:

Pradesh  and  the  daughters  are  at  Bilaspur,
Himachal  Pradesh.   Though  the  districts  are

very far.  The District Legal Services Authority,

ensure that the meeting of the petitioner and the
daughters proceeds at ease without any hurdle;
(c) The Secretaries, District Legal Services
Authorities, Mandi and Bilaspur either in person
or through an officer nominated by them shall get
in touch with the petitioner/mother- (Phoolan
Devi, Mobile No.8826990400) of the two girls;
(d) The girls are in the custody of their
paternal  grandfather  (Shri  Dandu  Ram,  Mobile
No.9418579929); and

time and the District Legal Services Authority,
Mandi, Himachal Pradesh will, after ascertaining
the suitable time at the end of the children,
arrange a meeting at a time and place to be

Karnataka High Court, which is presently under challenge. 
3. However, we may clarify that in the light of the law laid down
by this Court in Bangalore Development Authority & Anr. vs. The
State of Karnataka & Ors. 1, the acquisition of land to be made
by the Bangalore Development Authority2 under the provisions of
the Bangalore Development Authority Act, 1976 3, would be by
1  (2022) 1SCR 334
2  ‘BDA’, for short

application of the provisions of the  Land Acquisition Act,

by the Division Bench in paragraph 30(iii) of the impugned
order shall stand set aside, leaving it open to the BDA to take
recourse to acquisition of the land in question under the Act
of 1976 read with the Act of 1894.
4. We, however, reiterate the liberty granted by the Division
Bench as to the respondent’s entitlement to claim possession of
the land in the event acquisition proceedings are not commenced
and completed expeditiously.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
MISCELLANEOUS APPLICATION No.          OF 2026
(@ Diary No.37641 OF 2026)
IN
(CIVIL APPEAL No(s). 4596-4597 OF 2026)
MUKESH SINGH      NON-APPLICANT(S)/
      APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
THE ORIENTAL INSURANCE CO. LTD.             APPLICANT(S)/
    RESPONDENT No.1
BILKIS BEGUM   NON-APPLICANT(S)/
    RESPONDENT No.2
ORDER
1. We have heard learned counsel for the parties.
2. Delay condoned.
3. This Miscellaneous Application has been filed by
the  applicant-Respondent  No.1,  i.e.  the  Oriental
Insurance Co. Ltd., for clarification of the final
order  dated  20.04.2026  passed  by  this  Court  while
allowing  Civil  Appeal  No(s).4596-4597  of  2026,
preferred by appellant Mukesh Singh.
4. Appellant, as the claimant, had preferred a claim
petition before the Motor Accident Claims Tribunal for
the  injury  suffered  by  him  in  a  motor  vehicular
accident.
5. By the judgment and award dated 30.05.2013, the
1

--- Page 297 ---
Motor Accident Claims Tribunal awarded a compensation
of Rs.10,61,120/- to the appellant.
6. Seeking  enhancement  of  compensation,  appellant
approached the High Court by filing an appeal. High
Court vide the order dated 18.09.2013 dismissed the
said appeal.
7. Aggrieved thereby, appellant filed Special Leave
Petition (Criminal) No(s).14125-14126 of 2026 before
this Court.
8. On 21.11.2025, this Court had issued notice on the
Special  Leave  Petition(s)  as  well  as  on  the
Interlocutory Application for condonation of delay. It
was made clear that in the event delay was condoned and
compensation  was  enhanced,  appellant  would  not  be
entitled to receive interest for the period of delay.
9. Subsequently, on leave being granted, this Court
vide order dated 20.04.2026, allowed the two appeals
and enhanced the compensation from Rs.10,61,120/- to
Rs.40,61,600/-, along with interest at the rate of 7%
per annum on the enhanced compensation amount from the
date of filing of the claim petition within two months.
10. We find that the order of the High Court is dated
18.09.2013 whereas the Special Leave Petition(s) were
filed  on  08.10.2025.  There  was,  thus,  delay  of
approximately 12 years, to be precise 4228 days.
2

--- Page 298 ---
11. This  Court  while  issuing  notice  had  put  the
appellant on notice that in the event he succeeded in
the appeal, the period of delay would not be counted
for the purpose of award of interest on the enhanced
compensation.
12. In view thereof we clarify that the judgment and
order  of  this  Court  dated  20.04.2026  would  stand
modified to the extent that the interest of 7% per
annum  awarded  on  the  enhanced  compensation  of
Rs.40,61,600/- would not be available to the appellant-
claimant for the period of delay which is quantified to
be 4228 days.
13. With  this  clarification,  the  Miscellaneous
Application is allowed.
14. Pending  application(s),  if  any,  shall  stand
disposed of.
…………………………………………………...J.
      
  [UJJAL BHUYAN]
…………………………………………………...J.
     [ATUL S. CHANDURKAR]
NEW DELHI;
27th OCTOBER, 2026.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. The  petitioner before  this Court  has filed  the
present petition, being aggrieved by the impugned order
dated 23.01.2026 passed by the High Court of Judicature at
Bombay in Anticipatory Bail Application No. 3564 of 2025,
rejecting the prayer for anticipatory bail in connection
with FIR/Crime No. 767 of 2025, registered at Police
Station Vartak Nagar, District Thane, Maharashtra, for the
offences punishable under Sections 467, 409, 120-B, 420
read with Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860.
2. This Court, vide order dated  25.02.2026, granted
interim protection to the petitioner in the matter with
direction to join the investigation. It is not in dispute
that the petitioner has joined the investigation as and
when called upon by the Investigating Officer.
3. Learned counsel for the respondent-State submits
that  the  petitioner  has  failed  to  hand  over  certain
documents to the Investigating Officer.
4. Learned counsel for the petitioner clarifies that
the company in question has been admitted to Corporate
Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) / liquidation before
the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT), and an insolvency
2

--- Page 314 ---
Resolution Professional (IRP/RP) has taken over the affairs
and records of the company, leaving the petitioner with no
custody or control over the said records.
5. Having heard learned counsel for the parties and
upon perusal of the record, this Court is of the opinion
that the interim order dated 25.02.2026 deserves to be made
absolute.
6. Accordingly, interim order dated 25.02.2026 is made
absolute subject to the condition that petitioner shall
continue to co-operate with the investigation and shall
report  as  and  when  called  upon  to  do  so  by  the
Investigating Authority.
7. IA  No.  208801  of  2026,  has  been  preferred  by
respondent No. 2 seeking withdrawal/refund of the sum of
Rs. 1,00,00,000/- (Rupees One Crore) deposited by the
petitioner before this Court.
8. In the considered opinion of this court, respondent
No.  2  has  an  efficacious  remedy  to  establish  their
claim/dues before the NCLT. Without entering into the
merits of the financial claims, this Court declines to
order directing release of the said amount to respondent
No. 2.
9. The Registry of this Court is directed to transmit
the deposited amount of Rs. 1,00,00,000/- (Rupees One
3

--- Page 315 ---
Crore)  along  with  accrued  interest,  if  any,  to  the
concerned NCLT. Respondent No. 2 shall be at liberty to
file an appropriate application before the NCLT, which
shall be considered and decided in accordance with law.
10. The Special Leave Petition is accordingly disposed
of in the above terms.
11. Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand
disposed of.

5. The facts of the case reveal that the petitioners
were apprehended with 3.5 kg of ganja and 54 litres of
illicit liquor. They were convicted by the Trial Court for
offences punishable under Sections 8(c) read with Section
20(b)(ii)(B)  of  the  Narcotic  Drugs  and  Psychotropic
Substances Act, 1985 (for short, the “NDPS Act”), and
Section 34(2) of the Madhya Pradesh Excise Act, 1915, and
were sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for a
period of five years. Out of the substantive sentence of
five years’ rigorous imprisonment, the petitioners have
already  undergone  approximately  one  year  of  actual
incarceration.
6. Learned counsel for the petitioners submits that the
petitioners have been falsely implicated in the alleged
2

--- Page 318 ---
offence, there is every possibility of their acquittal, and
considering the period of incarceration undergone as well
as the grounds urged,  the execution of their sentences
deserves  to  be  suspended  during  the  pendency  of  the
criminal appeal before the High Court.
7. Per  contra,  learned  counsel  appearing  for  the
respondent-State  vehemently  opposes  the  prayer  for
suspension of sentence and grant of bail.
8. Having heard learned counsel for the parties and
taking into consideration the totality of the facts and
circumstances  as  well  as  the  period  of  incarceration
undergone,  this  Court  is  of  the  opinion  that  the
application  for  suspension  of  sentence  deserve  to  be
allowed.
9. Accordingly,  the  execution  of  the  substantive
sentence of imprisonment awarded to the petitioners shall
remain suspended during the pendency of the criminal appeal
before the High Court, and they are directed to be released
on bail, subject to such terms and conditions as may be
imposed by the Trial Court.

D.NO. 50814 OF 2025
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NO(S).            OF 2026
(@ SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (C) NO(S).           OF 2026) 
   [@ D.NO. 50814 OF 2025]
M/S BHARAT COKING COAL LIMITED                     Appellant(s)
                                VERSUS
M/S. ANNAPURNA CONSTRUCTION                        Respondent(s)
O R D E R
1. Delay condoned.
2. Leave granted.
3. This appeal is directed against the order dated 15.04.2025 by
which the High Court in a Petition filed by the appellant under
Article 227, affirmed the order dated 20.09.2022 passed by the
Executing Court and dismissed the writ petition. The High Court
held that the Executing Court was competent to interpret the award
for the purposes of execution. The High Court has negatived the
contention of the appellant, that the award does not mention the
date  from  which  the  interest  is  payable  on  the  award  and,
therefore, the respondent is entitled to interest with effect from
02.09.2005 i.e., the date on which the second award was passed. 
4. We have heard the learned counsel for the respective parties
at length.
1

--- Page 321 ---
D.NO. 50814 OF 2025
5. For the purpose of this appeal, suffice it to say that the
second award which was passed on 02.09.2005 and dealt with claim
nos. 7 and 11. The second award does not mention the date from
which the interest is payable. Therefore, as regards claim nos. 7
and 11, the interest is required to be computed in consonance with
Section 37(1)(b) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996.
Hence, it is clarified that the respondent shall be entitled to
interest insofar as claim nos. 7 and 11 are concerned from the date
of the second award i.e., 02.09.2005.
6. To the aforementioned extent, the orders passed by the High
Court and the Executing Court are modified.
7. Accordingly, the appeal is disposed of. 
8.  Pending  interlocutory  application(s),  if  any,  shall  stand
disposed of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL ORIGINAL JURISDICTION
TRANSFER PETITION (CIVIL) NO.2524 OF 2026
SHILPI BANSAL                        ...PETITIONER
Versus
SHUBHAM GARG                   ...RESPONDENT
O R D E R
The Transfer Petition is to transfer Matrimonial Case No.590 of 2024
filed by the respondent-husband for divorce under Section 13(1)(i-a) of
Hindu Marriage Act, 1955,  titled Shubham Garg v. Smt. Shilpi Bansal
w/o Shubham Garg , pending before the Principal Judge, Family Court,
Baghpat, Uttar Pradesh to the Court of Learned Principal Judge, Family
Court, Karkardooma, New Delhi.
2. We were told on the last date that there was a settlement between
the parties and, hence, we directed both the husband and the wife to
be personally present before us. On going through the settlement, we
were not happy, especially, since the mother had willingly given up the
custody of the two minor children aged 13 and 9 years to the father
and she also categorically conceded that she had no monetary claim.
We, hence, directed the parties to be present before us for interaction
in the Committee Room. 

--- Page 341 ---
2
3. We  first  interacted  with  the  petitioner-wife  and  then  with  the
respondent-husband as also with the learned Counsel appearing for the
parties. We were appalled by the allegations made by the petitioner-
wife, especially, regarding the threats levelled against her based on
video footages. In fact, when we separately talked with the respondent-
husband, his contention was that he had evidence by way of video
footage to indicate the infidelity of the petitioner-wife. This confirms the
allegation raised by the wife against the husband. We were convinced
that there was no settlement possible with our intervention and we
were not inclined to accept the settlement as placed before us. 
4. Hence,  we  reject  the  settlement  and  allow  the  transfer  of
Matrimonial Case No.590 of 2024 filed by the respondent-husband for
divorce  under  Section  13(1)(i-a)  of  Hindu  Marriage  Act,  1955, from
Principal Judge, Family Court, Baghpat, Uttar Pradesh to the Court of
Learned  Principal  Judge,  Family  Court,  Karkardooma,  New  Delhi,
wherein,  we  are  told,  a  petition  is  pending  as  Guardianship  Case
No.GP/01/2026. We request the Family Court, Karkardooma, New Delhi,
to take up both the matters together and also enable a maintenance
case to be filed by the wife, who has the custody of the children. The
wife shall be provided with effective and quality legal services.
5. In the meanwhile, considering the status of the parties, the wife
being unemployed and left to fend for herself and her children, whereas

--- Page 342 ---
3
the petitioner is having two shops inside Delhi, we are of the opinion
that a maintenance of Rs.15,000/- should be paid every month to the
wife and two children from the month of November, 2026, which shall
be paid within the 5 th of every month thereafter; subject only to the
orders  to  be  passed  in  the  maintenance  case  now  directed  to  be
initiated by the Family Court. 
6. We make it clear that the Family Court shall not proceed with the
matter unless the maintenance is paid every month.
7. We also caution the respondent-husband from uploading or making
viral any video footage with respect to the petitioner-wife, in which
event, the petitioner-wife would be entitled to move this Court directly
by an application in the above disposed of petition. Learned Counsel
appearing  for  the  petitioner-wife,  appointed  by  the  Legal  Services
Authority, has fairly consented to assist her, if such need arises.
8. The Transfer Petition is allowed with the above direction.
9. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand rejected.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
EXTRAORDINARY APPELLATE JURISDICTION
SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (CRL) NO.1698 OF 2026
M/s. Gauri Buildcon                       ...Petitioner(s)
Versus
The State of Telangana & Anr.   ...Respondent(s)
O R D E R
The High Court, by the impugned order, refused to quash the
chargesheet filed against the petitioner on a complaint filed by the
2nd respondent  finding  that  the  case  involved  diversion  of  huge
amounts, which can only be properly adjudicated in a trial.
2. T oday,  when  the  matter  was  taken  up  for  hearing,  learned
Counsel  for  the  respondent-State  informed  us  that,  despite  best
efforts, the 2 nd respondent could not be traced out. However, she
submits  that  the  chargesheet  has  been  filed  and  the  trial  would
commence immediately.
3. Learned Counsel for the petitioner, on the other hand, submits
that it was purely a commercial transaction, and if at all the 2 nd
respondent has a claim, he   could    seek   for    recovery   of
money.   There   is    absolutely     no     reason     to    find criminal
culpability on the petitioner and the criminal law is put in motion only
as a strong-arm tactic.

--- Page 345 ---
4. The chargesheet has been produced as Annexure P12, which
refers to the specific case of the 2 nd respondent, the complainant,
that  his  company,  House  of  Electronics,  paid  an  amount  of
Rs.4,15,35,000/- on 24.02.2023 to purchase Samsung mobile phones.
The contention is that despite accepting the money, the stock was
not  transferred  to  the  2nd respondent.  Obviously,  it  is  purely  a
commercial transaction and the petitioner’s remedy is by way of a
civil suit, which if not initiated till now, it is hit by limitation, since
three  years  have  passed  from  24.02.2023.  However,  if  there  is
anything  to  indicate  an  extension  of  limitation,  like  an
acknowledgement or a transaction after the date of initial transfer of
money, the 2 nd respondent would be entitled to file a civil suit for
recovery. 
5. We  make  it clear  that we have  not validated  the claim for
recovery,  nor  should  the  quashing  of  the  criminal  complaint  be
understood  as  having  accepted  the  petitioner’s  case  of  no  such
transaction having occurred. If a civil suit is filed, the matter could be
adjudicated  on  the  basis  of  the  evidence  filed  before  it  and  all
contentions of both parties are left open. The criminal complaint,
however, cannot be continued, since if permitted, it would be an
abuse of process of law.
6. We, hence, quash P12 chargesheet filed by the EOW T eam-VI,
CCS, DD, Hyderabad, pursuant to FIR No.153/2023 dated 03.05.2023

--- Page 346 ---
and direct that no further proceeding be taken on the same. 
7. The  Special  Leave  Petition  is  disposed  of  with  the  above
direction,  leaving  liberty to the 2 nd respondent to  file a civil suit,
subject to laws of limitation.
8. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand rejected.
