                             O R D E R
1. Heard learned counsel for the parties. We also interacted
with Ms.Ayesha Siddiqua Quadri-petitioner wife and Mr.Musaid
Ali Syed-respondent husband through video conferencing.
2. It  is  an  unfortunate  case  where  the  siblings  are
separated due to an ongoing dispute between the petitioner-
wife and respondent-husband. The petitioner-wife is living in
Latur, Maharashtra and the respondent-husband is in Hyderabad.
The respondent-husband informed us that he is working in Tech

--- Page 353 ---
2
Mahindra  Company  at  Hyderabad  with  a  take-home  pay  is
approximately  Rs.1,15,000/-  per  month.  There  are  three
children in the marriage. The elder daughter-Zabira is aged
nine years and she lives with the father. There are two boys,
namely, Hammad and Jawwad who are aged seven years and three
years respectively, are with the mother. The daughter is
undergoing school education in Hyderabad. The petitioner-
mother stated before us that she has admitted Hammad to an
international school at Latur and younger boy is three years
old.
3. Considering  that  the  daughter  is  at  Hyderabad,  the
respondent-husband shall allow video calls with the mother on
a daily basis at a time mutually agreed upon. Equally, the two
boys who are at Latur, cannot be deprived of the company of
the father. The father has graciously undertaken that he will
incur all their educational and medical expenses if any, for
the children.
4. We appreciate the stand taken by the respondent-father.
The mother shall, on daily basis, allow video calls to the
father with both the boys at a time mutually agreed upon.
5. This arrangement will continue till we make further
orders on 04th December, 2026.
6. Pending further talks between the parties and pending
arrangements with regard to the custody and visitation rights,
we are of the opinion that there is an immediate crisis at the
end of the petitioner-wife and the two boys which the Court
cannot shut its eyes. Admittedly, no maintenance has been paid

--- Page 354 ---
3
to the petitioner-wife till now.
7. Before we consider the matter further, we direct that
respondent-husband to pay a sum of Rs.5,00,000/- to the
petitioner-wife  directly  into  the  bank  account  of  the
petitioner-wife.
8. The  respondent-husband  undertakes  that  the  aforesaid
amount will be paid directly into the bank account of the
petitioner-wife in three installments.
9. The undertaking is placed on record.
10. The petitioner-wife shall file an affidavit with regard
to details of expenses for school education and other major
expenses that she has used the money for. 
11. We, however, grant time to the respondent-husband to pay
the aforesaid amount of Rs.5,00,000/- in the following terms:-
“1. Let the first installment of Rs.2,00,000/- be
paid on or before 30.11.2026.
2. Let the second installment of Rs.1,50,000/- be
paid on or before 15.01.2027.
3. Let the third installment of Rs.1,50,000/- be
paid on or before 28.02.2027.”

account details of the petitioner-wife to the learned counsel
for the respondent-husband, if not already available with the
respondent-husband.
13. In the meantime, parties, being fairly well-educated, are
requested to amicably resolve their dispute, even though
mediation has failed.

--- Page 355 ---
4
14. Parties have favourably responded to the suggestion of

husband paying a reasonable amount as compensation to the
petitioner-wife.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
Criminal Appeal  No(s).  /2026
@SLP (Crl.) No(s).   16429/2026
RANBIR @ RANVIR SINGH                              Appellant(s)
                                VERSUS
STATE OF HARYANA                                   Respondent(s)
O R D E R 
1. Leave granted.
2. Heard learned counsel for the parties.
3. This appeal arises from an order dated 27.01.2026
passed by the High Court of Punjab and Haryana at
Chandigarh rejecting the regular bail prayer of the
appellant  in  connection  with  FIR  No.  62/2014,
registered  at  P.S.  Hodal,  District  Palwal
(Haryana).
4. The submission of the learned counsel for the
appellant is that the appellant has been implicated
on the  basis of  confessional statement  of co-
accused and there is no incriminating recovery from
the appellant. It is contended that the High Court
has rejected the bail prayer of the appellant on
the ground that he had been absconding for about
nine years but the correct fact is that he was
1

--- Page 373 ---
never declared a proclaimed offender and there is
no material on record to indicate that any steps
taken were served on the appellant for securing his
presence.  Besides,  the  appellant  has  suffered
pending trial incarceration of a period exceeding
three and a half years. In such circumstances, it
is submitted, the appellant, who has no previous
criminal  antecedents,  may  be  released  on  bail
pending trial. 
5.  The learned Counsel for the State-respondent has
opposed the prayer for bail but could not dispute
that the implication of the appellant is based on
confessional statement of co-accused and he also
could not point out any document or evidence to
indicate  that  the  appellant  was  declared  a
proclaimed offender.
6. In such circumstances, having regard to the fact
that  the  appellant  has  suffered  pending  trial
incarceration exceeding three and a half years, we
are of the view that the appellant is entitled to
be released on bail at this stage.
7.  Accordingly, the appeal is allowed. The order
passed by the High Court rejecting the regular bail
prayer of the appellant is set aside.
8. The appellant shall be released on bail on such
terms and conditions as the trial court may deem
fit to impose in the facts and circumstances of the
2

--- Page 374 ---
case.
9. Pending  application(s),  if  any,  shall  stand
disposed of.
  
………………………………………………………………..J
[MANOJ MISRA]
………………………………………………………………..J
[MANMOHAN]
New Delhi;
October 27, 2026.

         UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
The Special Leave Petition challenges an order which
declined to interfere with the rejection of an application
under Section 9 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996.
 
2. We found no reason to interfere with the same, however,
we were curious as to whether any application under Section 11
of the Act of 1996 was moved, especially, when the High Court
noticed that there was no such application moved. We are
informed that an application has been moved before the High
Court of Judicature at Allahabad and has been pending for long
and there is no chance of it being considered in the near
future. Allegations were also made that the respondents were
constantly taking adjournment, which was stoutly denied by the
respondents.
2

--- Page 390 ---
SLP(C)  No. 25564/2025
3. In any event, since a dispute exists between the parties
and there is an application moved under Section 11, we were of
the opinion that an Arbitrator could be appointed by us.
However,  learned  Counsel  for  the  respondent  raised  a
contention that there was no arbitrable dispute and the
petitioner  cannot  claim  any  association,  much  less  a
partnership with the    respondent.
4. We would only clarify that all disputes could be raised
before the learned Arbitrator including the very contention
against the validity of constituting an Arbitration itself and
even  prayers  for  interim  orders  could  be  considered
independently, without being influenced by the impugned order
herein.
5. On  consent  of  the  parties,  we  appoint  Hon’ble  Smt.
Justice Chandrasekharan Sudha, Former Judge of the Delhi High
Court (Mobile No. +91 94460 45653) as the Arbitrator to
adjudicate upon the disputes that have arisen between the
parties. The learned Arbitrator shall issue notices to the
parties in connection with the arbitral proceedings. The
learned  Arbitrator  is  free  to  determine  her  fee  in
3

--- Page 391 ---
SLP(C)  No. 25564/2025
consultation with the parties. We make it clear that we have
expressed no opinion on the merits of the case, which aspect
is left open for the parties to urge before the learned
Arbitrator.
6. The  Registry  of  the  Court  shall  inform  the  Learned
Arbitrator.
7. With the aforesaid, the Special Leave Petition stands
disposed of.
8. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.
(CHANDRESH)                                     (POOJA SHARMA)

[Arising out of impugned final judgment and order dated  07-09-2026
in CRMM No. 50469/2026 passed by the High Court of Punjab & Haryana
at Chandigarh]
GURDEV SINGH & ANR.                                Petitioner(s)
                                VERSUS
THE STATE OF PUNJAB & ORS.                         Respondent(s)
IA No. 318176/2026 - EXEMPTION FROM FILING C/C OF THE IMPUGNED 
JUDGMENT
IA No. 318180/2026 - EXEMPTION FROM FILING O.T.
 
Date : 26-10-2026 This matter was called on for hearing today.
CORAM :  HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE SANDEEP MEHTA
         HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE DEVENDRA KUMAR UPADHYAYA
For Petitioner(s)  Mr. Chritarth Palli- 3235, AOR
                   Ms. Harsheen M Palli, Adv.
                   Mr. Agam Agarwal, Adv.
                   Mr. Rajat Gupta, Adv.
                   Ms. Anushka Juneja, Adv.
                   
                   
For Respondent(s)  
          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
The present proceeding has its genesis in FIR No. 221 dated 28 th
December, 2017, registered at Police Station Dehlon, Ludhiana for the
offences punishable under Sections 324, 323, 506, and 120B of the
Indian Penal Code, 1860 (for short, “IPC”), at the instance of one
Jorawar Singh against respondent Nos. 2 to 4.
 2. Respondent No. 4, in turn, lodged a cross case being DDR No. 10
dated 4 th January, 2018 for the offences punishable under Sections

--- Page 397 ---
2
325, 506, 201, and 34 of the IPC against five persons, including both
the petitioners.
3. Since the petitioners were working abroad, they were unable to
appear before the trial Court and were declared proclaimed offenders
on  22nd November,  2023  and  20th February,  2020  respectively.  It
seems that wiser counsel prevailed, and both sides decided to settle
their  disputes  amicably.  Accordingly,  the  proceedings  of  the  case
arising from DDR No. 10 of 2018 were compromised and the High
Court  quashed  those  proceedings  qua three  co-accused  who  were
arraigned along with the petitioners. Likewise, the proceedings of FIR
No. 221 of 2017 were also quashed qua respondent Nos. 2 to 4 after
due verification of the compromise by the Magistrate. The quashing of
the FIR as well as the cross case was made subject to the deposit of
Rs.  10,000/-  with  Ashiana  (Specialized  Adoption  Agency)  and
Snehalaya for Girls (Children’s Home) QQ 2C-t-437, 15 C, Sector 15,
Chandigarh,  160015  by  three  co-accused  persons  and  respondent
Nos. 2 to 4 respectively.
4. Thereafter,  the  petitioners  and  respondent  Nos.  2  to  4  also
entered into a compromise which was recorded on 4 th February, 2025.
Based on the said compromise, the petitioners approached the High
Court with CRM-M-50469-2026 seeking quashing of the proceedings
of the case bearing DDR No. 10 of 2018 as well as the proclamation
orders dated 20th February, 2020 and 22nd November, 2023.
5. In these proceedings before the High Court, respondent Nos. 2 to
4 being  the  injured persons  and  the  complainant  in  DDR No. 10
appeared  through  their  counsel  and  affirmed  the  execution  of  the
compromise  dated  4th February,  2025.  Noting  the  same,  the  High
Court  vide  impugned order dated 7 th September, 2026, directed the

--- Page 398 ---
3
parties  to  appear  before  the  trial  Court/Illaqa Magistrate  on  28th
September, 2026 or any other date convenient to the said Court for
getting  their  respective  statements  recorded  with  regard  to  the
compromise. The concerned Court was thereupon directed to submit a
detailed  report  regarding  the  compromise  arrived  at  between  the
parties.
6.  Learned counsel for the petitioners urged that the petitioners are
ready  and  willing  to  participate  in  the  compromise  verification
proceedings  but  requiring  their  personal  presence  before  the
Magistrate would jeopardise the job prospects of the petitioners who
are working abroad and in addition thereto, the petitioners would be
put under unnecessary financial burden. It was thus submitted that
the petitioners may be allowed to appear in the proceedings before the
Magistrate  through  virtual  mode/video  conferencing  with  due
representation through counsel.
7. Learned  counsel  further  submitted that,  to  demonstrate  their
bona fides  and intent to act as good Samaritans, the petitioners are
ready to deposit a sum of Rs.5 lakhs with the same institution which
caters to children with specialised needs as is referred to in the earlier
quashing petitions of the co-accused persons as well as respondent
Nos. 2 to 4.
8. Suffice it to say that for verification of the compromise in a case
involving compoundable offences, only the presence and consent of
the  complainant  is  mandatory.  There  would  be  no  requirement  of
presence of the accused to verify the compromise.  In any event, since
the proceedings against the co-accused persons have already been
quashed by the High Court based on the compromise, allowing the
proceedings  against  the  petitioners  to  continue,  despite  the

--- Page 399 ---
4
undisputed fact that the complainants have settled the dispute with
them, would be a sheer wastage of judicial time.
9. In view of the peculiar facts noted above, we hereby provide that
the  petitioners  herein  shall  appear  before  the  Magistrate  in  the
compromise verification proceedings to be carried out in terms of order
dated 7th September, 2026 passed by the learned Single Judge of the
High Court by the virtual mode. The Court shall not insist for physical
presence of the petitioners in these proceedings.
10. Consequently,  we  provide  that  the  personal  presence  of  the
petitioners shall not be insisted upon in the compromise verification
proceedings to be conducted before the Magistrate.  The petitioners
shall  appear  before  the  Magistrate  through  virtual  mode/video
conferencing on the date fixed, subject to their identification by their
respective  Advocates.  Before  the  proceedings  of  verification  of
compromise are conducted, the petitioners shall be required to deposit
a sum of Rs.5 lakhs with the institution named Ashiana (Specialized
Adoption Agency) and Snehalaya for Girls (Children’s Home) QQ 2C-
437, 15C, Sector 15, Chandigarh-160015. The compromise verification
proceedings  shall  be  undertaken  after  the  proof  of  payment  of
aforesaid amount is placed before the trial Court concerned.
11. With these directions, the special leave petition stands disposed
of.
12. Pending applications, if any, shall stand disposed of.
(VARSHA MENDIRATTA)                         (AKSHAY KUMAR BHORIA)

1. Given the subject matter of the writ petition filed before the
High Court of Judicature at Allahabad in Writ-C No. 7817/2025,
transfer of which is sought presently, and as the very same
issues  that  arise  for  consideration  therein  are  already
pending consideration before this Court in Civil Appeal No.

this transfer petition deserves to be and is, accordingly,
allowed. The said writ petition shall stand transferred to the

High Court in the said writ petition with regard to deposit of

the Registry  of the High Court.

1016/2025, the High Court shall transfer the aforestated
amount deposited with its Registry to the Registry of this
Court.
4. Upon the said amount being received, the Registry of this
Court shall invest the same in an interest-bearing fixed
deposit account with auto-renewal clause in a nationalized
bank.  
5. As pending applications in the said writ petition would also
stand transferred to this Court, it would be open to the

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL ORIGINAL JURISDICTION
TRANSFER PETITION (CRL.) NO. 967 OF 2026
MOHAMMED AFZAL                             PETITIONER
                        VERSUS
M/S PNB METLIFE INDIA INSURANCE CO. LTD                  RESPONDENT
O R D E R
1. Heard learned counsel for the petitioner.
2. The sole ground raised in this Transfer Petition relates to
the field of inconvenience.
3. In view of the decision of this Court by a Division Bench in
”M/s Shri Sendhur Agro & Oil Industries vs. Kotak Mahindra Bank
Ltd. in TP (Crl.) No. 608/2024 reported in 2025 INSC 328”, it was
laid  down  that  inconvenience  alone  cannot  be  a  ground  for
successfully seeking a transfer of a pending case from one State
to the other. The relevant extract of the said judgment is
reproduced below:
“xxxx         xxxx            xxxx
65. For the purpose of transfer of any case or
proceedings under Section 406 of the Cr.P.C., the
case must fall within the ambit of the expression
“expedient  for  the  ends  of  justice”.  Mere
inconvenience or hardship that the accused may
have to face in travelling from Coimbatore to
Chandigarh would not fall within the expression
“expedient for the ends of justice”. The case must
fall within any of the five situations as narrated
in para 49 of this judgment. It is always open for
1

--- Page 439 ---
the petitioner accused to pray for exemption from
personal appearance or request the Court that he
may be permitted to join the proceedings online.
xxxx            xxxx            xxxx”
4. In view of the above, since no good ground is made out, the
Transfer Petition stands dismissed.
5. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.
.................J.
  (SHEEL NAGU)
NEW DELHI;
OCTOBER 26, 2026.

the State.

correctness of the order  dated 13-08-2026 in SBCRMBA
No. 10062/2026 passed by the High Court of Judicature

--- Page 454 ---
2
for  Rajasthan  at  Jaipur.  By  the  said  order,  the
petitioner has been denied the benefit of bail in
connection  with  FIR  No.349/2021  registered  with
Karghani/Kardhani  Police  Station,  Jaipur  West,
Rajasthan, for the offences punishable under Sections
498A, 406, 384, 302 and 120-B of the Indian Penal Code,
1860(for  short,  ‘IPC’).  After  investigation,  the
petitioner was charge-sheeted under Sections 498-A &
306 of the IPC by charge sheet No.135/2026 dated
02.07.2026.
3. Learned counsel for the petitioner submits that the
deceased  had  died  on  07.03.2021  and  the  FIR  was
registered on 20.04.2021 after delay of nearly 44 days;
that the marriage was of 2008 and the death was 13
years after; that the Sections invoked are 498A & 306
of the IPC; that the petitioner has been in custody
since 12.06.2026 and even though the FIR was filed on
20.04.2021,  there  was  no  interim  protection  till
04.12.2023, the petitioner was not taken into custody.
4. Learned counsel for the State, however, vehemently
opposes the bail prayer of the petitioner.
5. Considering overall facts and circumstances of the
case; having perused the records and the period already
undergone by the petitioner, we are inclined to enlarge
the petitioner on bail pending trial.
6. Accordingly, we direct that petitioner shall be
enlarged  on  bail  pending  trial,  subject  to  the

--- Page 455 ---
3
satisfaction of the concerned Trial Court in connection
with  the  aforesaid  charge  sheet/FIR  and  for  the
offences mentioned hereinabove.

above terms.

disposed of.

        UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. The Petitioner herein has been apprehended in connection
with FIR No. 122/2021 for offences under Sections 20(b)
(ii)(c)  &  8  of  the  Narcotic  Drugs  and  Psychotropic
Substances Act, 1985 (for short, “the NDPS Act”). The FIR
was registered pursuant to 219.55 Kg of Ganja being found
in an abandoned car bearing Registration No. CG-05-5214.
Upon investigation, it was found that the car in question
was rented out in the name of co-accused Lukesh who
further disclosed the name of the Petitioner on whose
behalf he claimed to have carried the Ganja. 
2. It has been argued by the counsel for the Petitioner that
there  are  several  inconsistencies  in  the  procedure
adopted  by  the  Investigating  authorities,  the  most
glaring of which has been made out during the course of
trial regarding the admission of 2 of the independent
SLP(Crl.)  No.  19637/2026 2

--- Page 530 ---
witnesses PW1 & PW2 having signed blank sheets of paper
during the recovery and sampling process.
3. Upon a perusal of the material on record, we are inclined
to grant bail, as the Petitioner has been languishing in
jail for over a year with his nexus to the crime solely
dependant upon the disclosure of the co-accused. Further,
the trial proceedings seems unlikely to be concluded
soon.
4. In view of the reasons mentioned hereinabove, we order
that the Petitioner be released on bail subject to such
terms and conditions that the Jurisdictional Trial Court
may deem fit to impose.
5. With the above directions, the Special Leave Petition is
disposed of.
6. Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand disposed
of.

         HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE K. VINOD CHANDRAN

Upon hearing the counsel, the Court made the following
O R D E R
The above petition was filed against the order of
the High Court, which sustained the order of the Trial
Court dated 15.07.2026, in the suit filed by the
petitioner herein, modifying the status quo order dated
1

--- Page 580 ---
31.07.2025,  which  was  confirmed  after  contest  on
04.09.2025  and  permitting  the  respondent-Club  to
celebrate the ensuing Durga Puja on the suit property
by erecting Puja Pandal, with direction to remove the
same  immediately  after  completion  of  puja.  The
modification by the High Court in the revision filed
was only with respect to a direction to the Civil Court
to appoint an Advocate Commissioner to ensure that the
temporary  structures  constructed  therein  are
dismantled. 
2. We granted a stay of the impugned orders and today
we are told that the matter has become infructuous
since Durga Puja is over, however, the suit is still
pending  and  the  petitioner  prays  that  it  may  be
expedited. 
3. The suit was filed for declaring the absolute
ownership of the plaintiff over the plaint scheduled
property  and  declaring  that  the  defendant  has
absolutely no right, title or interest over the said
property.  The  suit  produced  in  the  Special  Leave
Petition as Annexure P5 also sought for a perpetual
injunction  against  organizing  Durga  Puja in  the
plaintiff’s  premises  and  an  order  for  removal  of
temporary  structures  erected,  as  also  perpetual
injunction  restraining  the  defendant-Club  from
2

--- Page 581 ---
disturbing the peaceful possession of the plaintiffs.
4. We are told by the respondent-Club that the Durga
Puja was conducted on the basis of an agreement, which
we  find  at  Annexure  R1.  We  find  absolutely  no
consideration and the agreement also is unstamped.
Further, the terms indicate that the plaintiff is
obliged  to  keep  vacant  forever  a  portion  of  the
property for performing annual  Durga Puja , which we
find prima facie to be unconscionable.
5. In any event, the suit is pending and we are of
the opinion that it should be expedited. The Trial
Court shall keep in mind our observations regarding the
agreement when disposing of the suit.
6. The Special Leave Petition is disposed of.
7. Pending  application(s),  if  any,  shall  stand
rejected.
(HARPREET KAUR)                               (POOJA SHARMA)
COURT MASTER (SH)                           COURT MASTER (NSH)

this Court that the other co-accused persons named in the
FIR have been granted bail. This Court is not commenting
upon the bail order(s) passed by the High Court in respect
of the co-accused persons. So far as the petitioner is
concerned, there are specific allegations against the
petitioner, and a weapon has been recovered. Therefore,
this Court does not find any reason to allow the
application for grant of bail. The special leave petition
is dismissed. The trial court is requested to expedite the
trial and conclude the same at an early date.

1. Permission to file Special Leave Petition is granted.
2. Delay condoned.
1

--- Page 607 ---
3. The petitioner, a victim of systemic cheating and financial
fraud, challenges order dated 14.11.2025 passed by the High Court
of Delhi, whereby bail has been granted to the first respondent,
who is one of the accused.
4. The grounds urged to seek cancellation of bail are,  inter
alia, that the first respondent poses a flight risk, and the co-
accused person who was also granted bail has already absconded to
Dubai. The submission, thus, is that there are chances that the
first respondent will also escape the consequences of law. It is
also argued that the High Court has not imposed rigorous conditions
while  granting  bail  and  certain  instances  of  misuse  of  the
concession of bail have emerged.
5. Though the brilliant young lawyer representing the petitioner
has argued the case at length, almost persuading our interference
with the impugned order, it appears to us that instead of calling
upon the first respondent at this stage, the interests of the
petitioner and other victims of the crime can be adequately
protected by disposing of this Special Leave Petition with the
following directions:
(i) The first respondent is directed to deposit his original
passport with the investigating agency, if not already done.
He shall also file an affidavit stating that no other passport
has been obtained by him in his original name or any other
name;
(ii) In the event that there are instances of misuse of the
concession of bail, the petitioner or the prosecution shall be
at liberty to seek cancellation of bail by approaching the
2

--- Page 608 ---
High Court;
(iii)The  investigating  agency  is  directed  to  attach  the
immovable properties of respondent No. 1 or his associates as
a security measure; and
(iv) Respondent No. 1 shall not make any direct or indirect
attempt to influence witnesses or tamper with evidence.
6. The Special Leave Petition is, accordingly, disposed of.
7. Pending applications, if any, also stand disposed of.
(ARJUN BISHT)                             (PREETHI DILEEP KUMAR)
ASTT. REGISTRAR-cum-PS                        DY. REGISTRAR

               S U P R E M E  C O U R T  O F  I N D I A
                       RECORD OF PROCEEDINGS
Petition for Special Leave to Appeal (Crl.) No. 20370/2026
[Arising out of impugned final judgment and order dated 03-09-2026
in CRLM No. 59197/2026 passed by the High Court of Judicature at
Patna]
SHAMBHU SAHANI @SHAMBHU KUMAR@SHAMBHU KUMAR SAHANI   Petitioner(s)
                                VERSUS
THE STATE OF BIHAR                                   Respondent(s)
(FOR ADMISSION  AND IA No. 325623/2026 - EXEMPTION FROM FILING
O.T.)
 
Date : 27-10-2026 This matter was called on for hearing today.
CORAM : 
         HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE SANJAY KUMAR
         HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE SANJEEV SACHDEVA
For Petitioner(s) Mr. Awanish Sinha- 1671, AOR
                   Mr. Prem Ranjan Kumar, Adv.
                   Mr. Desh Ratan Nigam, Adv.
                   Mr. Sanjib Kumar Mohanthy, Adv.
                                      
For Respondent(s) Mr. Amit Chaudhary, Adv. 
Mr. Aagam Kaur, AOR
Mr. Kartikey, Adv. 
Ms. Nisha Bhaskar, Adv.  
           UPON hearing the counsel, the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
We find from the impugned order that the learned counsel who
appeared for the petitioner stated before the High Court that the
petitioner, Shambhu Sahani @ Shambhu Kumar @ Shambhu Kumar Sahani,
had one past criminal antecedent.  No mention of any past case has
been made in this special leave petition. 
In the light of the law laid down by this Court in “Munnesh
1

--- Page 652 ---
vs. State of Uttar Pradesh”1, the suppression of this fact is fatal
to the case of the petitioner. 
The special leave petition is, accordingly, dismissed on this
short ground. 
We may note that the issue of suppression of past criminal
antecedents keeps coming up time and again before this Court in
special leave petitions filed for anticipatory bail/regular bail.
It would be appropriate that the Registry insist upon an entry
being made, as a matter of course,  in the Synopsis/Listing
Proforma under the heading ‘Criminal Antecedents’ to ascertain
whether a petitioner who seeks anticipatory bail/regular bail has
any past criminal cases and if so, to furnish full details thereof,
including cases in which he/she has been acquitted. This procedure
shall be followed without fail in all future cases. 
A copy of this order shall be forwarded to the Registrar
(Judicial) of this Court for ensuring compliance. 
Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.
  (BABITA PANDEY)                           (PREETI SAXENA)
AR-CUM-PS                              COURT MASTER (NSH)

SUNEEL KUMAR AHIRWAR                               Petitioner(s)

(IA No. 322817/2026 - CONDONATION OF DELAY IN FILING SLP, IA
No. 322819/2026 - CONDONATION OF DELAY IN REFILING SLP AND IA
No. 322815/2026 - EXEMPTION FROM FILING O.T.)
 
Date : 28-10-2026 This matter was called on for hearing today.
CORAM : 
         HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE J.B. PARDIWALA
         HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE K. VINOD CHANDRAN
For Petitioner(s) : 
                   Mr. Ankur Rastogi, Adv.
                   Mrs. Priya Rastogi, Adv.
                   Mr. Kamal Mohan Gupta- 1269, AOR                
For Respondent(s) : 
          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. Delay condoned.
2. Exemption Application is allowed.
3. Heard Mr. Ankur Rastogi, the learned counsel appearing for the
petitioner. 
4. We take notice of the fact that on the very same day when the
impugned Order was passed, one another Order came to be passed by
the same learned Judge of the High Court in application under
Section 528 BNSS No.13328 of 2026 wherein in para 5, the Court
observed thus:-
“5. Learned counsel next submitted that the applicant had never
contacted any of the accused persons, nor met them in the past,
and had no direct or indirect connection with them in any manner

--- Page 804 ---
2
whatsoever. It was further submitted that the applicant is not a
beneficiary, whether in whole or in part, of any alleged illegal
payments made to the accused persons, and that no evidence has
been found against him during the course of investigation. Learned
counsel for applicant further submitted that there is hardly any
evidence against applicant to corroborate them with the alleged
incident. It has also been argued by learned counsel for applicant
that  without  conducting  fair  investigation,  the  concerned
Investigating  Officer  submitted  chargesheet  against  applicant
whereupon  without  applying  its  judicial  mind,  learned  court
concerned took cognizance of offence over the said chargesheet
which is abuse of process of law and as such, same may be
quashed.”
5. The High Court while  observing so, proceeded to quash the
criminal proceedings against the applicant therein. 
6. While on the very same FIR, the present petitioner also prayed
for quashing, however, the quashing was declined.
7. We need some clarification in this regard from the State.
8. Issue notice, returnable in four weeks. 
9. Dasti service, in addition, is permitted.
10. Liberty is granted to serve the Standing counsel for the State
of U.P.
